speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party House Leader; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a question to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons. First, however, I would like to congratulate him and say that we welcome his appointment as the minister responsible for the business of the House. We are confident he will draw on his many skills to work with his opposition colleagues in this House, in a manner that is constructive and in the best interests of Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, my point of order concerns Standing Order 7(3), which I will read to you. It is about the Chairman of Committees of the Whole-in other words, the Deputy Speaker of the House:
The Member so elected as Deputy Speaker and Chairman of Committees of the Whole shall continue to act in that capacity until the end of the Parliament for which he or she is elected, and in the case of a vacancy by death, resignation or otherwise, the House shall proceed forthwith to elect a successor.
Could the minister inform the House whether he intends to consult the opposition, as is customary and in keeping with parliamentary tradition, before moving the motion to elect a Deputy Speaker of the House?

speakeroldname: Hon. Harvie Andre (Minister of State to Prime Minister and Government House Leader):
speakerposition: Minister of State (Without Portfolio); Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, cognizant of the standing order and its requirements, and because of the fact that we had a recess since the elevation of the former Deputy Speaker to cabinet, the Prime Minister has not had an opportunity to have the usual discussions with the leaders of the Opposition. It is his intention to do so, after which he will have a recommendation hopefully agreed to with opposition leaders to bring to the House for election to Deputy Speaker. It is only for that reason that there is a delay.

Mr. Speaker, I too want to echo the concerns of my hon. colleague from Ottawa-Vanier. The point he raises is most appropriate.
I also wish to take this occasion to welcome my good friend from Calgary Centre in his new position. It appears as if there is a bit of an Alberta Mafia developing here in the government. We have the member for Calgary Centre, the member for Peace River and the member for Calgary West, all playing a critical role on the government benches. We look forward to an ongoing close working relationship with the team.

I rise today at the first opportunity after the break on a point of order, Mr. Speaker, to suggest firstly that debate on the budget motion be suspended and, second, to request that you carefully review the government bill currently on notice and determine whether or not the House should proceed with that bill at this time.
On Tuesday, February 20, the government presented its budget and moved the traditional motion to approve the measures it contains. A debate on this motion and the traditional amendments took place on subsequent days of that week.
Since that debate was last adjourned a significant event has in fact taken place. The Government of

March 5, 1990
Points of Order
British Columbia has approached the courts and asked for a ruling on the legitimacy of one of the major components of that budget, namely the Canada Assistance Plan.
Specifically, the province of British Columbia is asking the Court of Appeal to answer the following questions.
First, has the Government of Canada any statutory prerogative or contractual authority to limit its obligation under the Canada Assistance Plan Act, RSC 1970, Chapter C-l and its agreement with the Government of British Columbia dated March 23, 1967 to contribute 50 per cent of the cost to British Columbia for assistance and welfare services?
Second, do the terms of the agreement dated March 23, 1967 between the Governments of Canada and British Columbia, the subsequent conduct of the Government of Canada pursuant to the agreement and the provisions of the Canada Assistance Plan Act, RSC 1970, Chapter C-l give rise to a legitimate expectation that the Government of Canada would introduce no bill into Parliament to limit its obligation under the agreement or act without the consent of the people and Government of British Columbia?
Those questions are contained in Order in Council No. 287 signed by the Lieutenant-Governor on February 27, 1990.
I have forwarded a copy of the Order in Council and all relevant court documents that I have been able to obtain to the Chair.
We know that the first court hearing on this issue will take place tomorrow afternoon. I hope you will agree, Mr. Speaker, that the House should do all that it can to ensure that this hearing is as fair to the citizens of British Columbia as is possible.
I think it is important at this point for the House to remember the pledge it made some decades ago when it established the Canada Assistance Plan and defined the federal responsibility over welfare assistance, child care and other related issues.
Section 8 of the Canada Assistance Plan Act states: "an agreement may be amended or terminated by mutual consent of the minister and the provinces" and
"Canada may at any time give to the province notice of intention to terminate an agreement-the agreement shall cease to be effective for any period after the day fixed in the notice or for any period after the expiration of one year from the date on which the notice is given, whichever is the later."
Historically the House has by convention restrained itself from discussing questions which are before the courts when such a discussion would prejudice the outcome of those proceedings.
I refer of course to the sub judice convention.
Beauchesne's fifth and sixth editions describe the responsibility of members to exercise restraint in the following way:
Members are expected to refrain from discussing matters that are before the courts or tribunals which are courts of record. The purpose of this sub judice convention is to protect the parties in a case awaiting or undergoing trial and persons who stand to be affected by the outcome of a judicial inquiry. It is a voluntary restraint imposed by the House upon itself in the interest of justice and fair play.
As a result of the cases brought before it the House has a much clearer understanding of the sub judice convention as it applies to criminal cases than civil ones.
But the premise of the convention that everyone is entitled to a fair hearing before the courts without prejudicial debate in the Commons surely applies equally to criminal and civil matters.
I hope you will permit me, Mr. Speaker, to explain why I feel it should apply in today's circumstances.
The courts are being asked to judge whether there is a legitimate expectation that the Government of Canada would introduce no bill into Parliament to limit its obligation without the consent of British Columbia. It is also being asked whether the government has any authority to limit its contributions.
These two questions are part and parcel of the motion currently before the House. If the House resolves its approval for the budget, it will be endorsing the authority of the government to limit its contributions.
If the House gives leave to introduce any bill which reduces the Canada Assistance Plan to any or all provinces, it will be asserting that there is no "legitimate expectation that the government would introduce no bill".
March 5, 1990

How could the adoption of the budget motion fail to prejudice the rights of the citizens of British Columbia to a fair hearing on their questions?
Would it be fair for the government to be given the opportunity to put on the public record four days of evidence without the Government of British Columbia being able to have the opportunity to rebut or question that evidence or forward some of its own?
Similarly, to allow the bill on notice, if it indeed does limit payments under the Canada Assistance Plan, would prejudice the same appeal. It would also breach parliamentary tradition.
Beauchesne's sixth edition at paragraph 508, clause 4 reminds us that:
The reference of a bill to the Supreme Court of Canada withdraws
that bill temporarily from the jurisdiction of Parliament-The
question cannot be before two public bodies at the same time.
Beauchesne's cites a 1948 ruling that is germane to the question before us at the moment. At that time the Speaker was asked to accept an amendment to a government motion to appoint a joint committee of the House and Senate to consider the question of human rights and freedoms. The amendment proposed would have called for a reference to the Supreme Court of a general question of federal jurisdiction over the freedoms of speech, assembly, et cetera.
The Speaker at that time disallowed the amendment saying that "this amendment actually proposes that the Supreme Court be asked to consider the same matter that the main motion proposes to refer to a select committee. It seems to me that both these propositions cannot be approved at the same time by the House. If the constitutional situation of human rights is submitted to the Supreme Court, it thereby becomes sub judice and cannot be considered by the committee until the court has given its decision. The question cannot be before two public bodies at the same time."
I submit that if the debate on the budget motion proceeds, and if the bill currently on notice is in fact introduced, this is exactly what will ensue. Two public bodies, each trusted with responsibilities over justice, will have before them these questions about the legitimacy of the proposed termination of agreements under the Canada Assistance Plan.
Points of Order
Before I conclude, allow me to address briefly the sub judice convention itself. It strikes me that every time a public issue is before the courts, the House is buffeted by opposing whims on how the convention should be applied, whether the convention should be applied, why it should be applied, and so on.
Should such a re-examination occur today, I submit that it should not be material to your decision, Mr. Speaker, or the decision of the House to suspend voluntarily debate on the budget motion.
Nor should it colour your decision on whether or not to allow the bill currently on notice to proceed, because the convention does exist and it continues to be applied.
For example, only last summer, Mr. Speaker, you interjected to remind the House of its self-imposed restraint when members of the Opposition attempted to question the government on its decision to lay charges against Mr. Doug Small and the conflicting evidence given to the House committee.
In fact, since I have been in the House, I can only remember sub judice being applied to prevent the Opposition from unrestrainedly asking questions of the government on topical issues of the day.
Although it may sometimes appear so, the convention does not exist to protect the government. It exists to protect those before the courts.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I ask you to protect the interests of the citizens of British Columbia whose elected representatives are challenging, on their behalf, the budget measures proposed by this government.
I ask for debate on the budget motion to be suspended and for any proceedings on any bill regarding the Canada Assistance Plan to be stopped until such time as debate will not imperil the rights of these citizens from British Columbia to a fair hearing.

Mr. Speaker, I just want to make a couple of comments on the point raised by the member for Kamloops, House leader for the New Democratic Party.
Indeed he may have a point. The government could be breaking the law or possibly has broken the law already, but in my view this is a matter of law and not a matter for the Speaker of the House of Commons to settle. The courts are indeed empowered to look into these matters,

March 5, 1990
Business of the House
and I take it that both provinces at this time have taken measures to make their case in front of the courts.
I am therefore uncomfortable as to whether in your position as Speaker of this House, knowing our traditions and our customs, you should be ruling at this time on a matter of law. I know you cannot.
Therefore I put it simply to the House that although I agree with the member that there could be a good legal case made before the courts for the government breaking or being in breach of its agreements, or of its subagreements for that matter, at this time I must say that the Official Opposition would feel that the matter is a legal one, not one for the House.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I could just very quickly respond to the opening comments of the member for Kamloops by saying that I hope he does not think that because there are four Albertans involved it takes four Albertans to match wits with one British Columbian or one Ontarian. That is not the circumstance.
I indicated that we had no previous warning of this point of order so I am not in a position to reply in detail, except to dig back into my memory and recall, without the specific citation, previous speakers pointing out the fact that if this point of order were to prevail, then by the simple expedient of filing a lawsuit anybody could prevent the House of Commons from dealing with its normal business. That clearly would be an unacceptable situation. For that reason if for no others-and there certainly are other reasons-I would say this is rather a spurious point of order and probably not worthy.
If the Chair should see in the arguments more merit than is obvious to me at this point in time, I would ask that we have an opportunity to respond in detail. I have to say at this time I agree with my friend from Ottawa- Vanier that this point of order is elaborate and articulate but without merit in terms of substance.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. member for Kamloops has raised a very interesting point. It is public knowledge, as has been repeated by the hon. member for Kamloops, that at least one province is challenging in the courts
certain provisions which the federal government has enunciated in its budget speech.
The challenge lies on the side of civil law, not criminal law. The sub judice convention has never been as rigorously applied in civil matters as in criminal matters. Hon. members will know that as a consequence of matters raised by members to me recently, I have had to deal, with the sub judice convention with respect to criminal matters, and I think that position is quite clear.
I echo the words of the hon. House leader, that the hon. member for Kamloops put forward a very able argument. I want to consider carefully the reference to a particular ruling which the hon. member cited. I will take that matter under advisement and report back to the House as soon as I can.
However, in the meantime, I do not think it would be appropriate to delay the debate on the budget motion. We are not debating a bill at the moment. I have the hon. member's point. I will give it very careful consideration and will report back to the House as soon as I can.

The Budget

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am honoured and extremely pleased to be able to address the whole question of the budget this afternoon.
As I begin to do so, I would like to quote for the record a communication I have just received from a colleague addressing this very question. It reads as follows:
This budget is a true Tory budget. The government's real agenda, about which it said nothing in the last election campaign, is now fully visible, and the vast majority of Canadians are clearly unhappy about the directions in which the government is taking our countiy. In the last campaign the government did not talk about a deficit out of control. It did not promise reductions to unemployment insurance, health care funding, and education funding. It did not promise a clawback of old age security. When the Liberals said these were exactly the things that would happen, the Conservatives called them liars and fear-mongers.
If we were to ask Canadians today who are the liars and who are the fear-mongers, I suspect we would get a very different answer from the one that would have been given some months ago.
The member of Parliament for Winnipeg North, in an address a few days ago with respect to the budget, indicated that a budget reflects a government's priorities and is really a reflection of its very soul.
I was interested in that particular comment because, in a sense, it has profound implications. How I spend my money is actually a very important statement about what it is that I consider my priorities to be. What is it that is most important and what is it that is perhaps of lesser importance?
If you look at the government's budget from that perspective, you will find some very interesting facts that I want to share with this House. Defence spending will in fact increase by 5 per cent. The operations of CSIS, the Canadian Security Intelligence Service, will be increasing by 20 per cent.
I could give some other examples but I believe that those serve to make the point I want to make. It is that there are certain programs of government that will be getting substantial assistance.
Where are the largest cuts being made? To health care and to education. I could mention several others but I am going to concentrate on those two because they happen to be massive.
Let me talk very quickly and briefly about the reductions in transfer payments, particularly those with respect to education. They are even more severe when one looks at them in the total context within which they were taken. Education will suffer from the goods and services tax when it is implemented in 1991.
Hon. members will recall the postal subsidies from which education was exempted. Educational institutions were given these postal subsidies by a former minister of this government for scholarly and research journals. That promise was not honoured. Those dollars will have to be absorbed within current funding. In fact, there will be reductions in funding.
There are reductions in training and retraining. Supposedly that was a high priority of government. There are reductions in expenditures in science and technology. There again we keep hearing the rhetoric about the importance of those particular programs. There are reductions in student aid, which has seen no change since 1984. An administrative fee has been tacked on for those who need funding most.
What is the message being sent to students? The government is saying quite clearly that they have a lot, apart from its other decisions about reducing job opportunities for the summer. It is saying that they have too much. Otherwise, it would not be making those particular reductions.
In looking at education and health, the Association of University Teachers has estimated that there will be 39 billion fewer dollars from 1986 to 1995 in current government projections. With the reductions in 1986, after the government had said that it would not touch the formula, and with the intended reductions in 1989-90, which were not necessary because of the freezes that were imposed during this current budgetary year, there will be 39 billion fewer dollars for Canadians, for the provinces in health and education. There is roughly $9 billion less for education out of those $39 billion. I would suggest that there is well over another $1 billion of additional reductions elsewhere in other cuts.
Let us look at Manitoba alone where there will be 99 million fewer dollars for health and education over the next two years because of this budget. Let me tell you, ladies and gentlemen, you can buy a lot of health and education in Manitoba for $99 million.
March 5, 1990

Let us look at the message that this government is giving with respect to its reductions in health. What is the message to the elderly and to those who need health care? Obviously, it is saying: "If you do get sick or if you do need health care, it is going to be more costly and risky." Obviously, the supports that were there are no longer there. The system is deteriorating. People are waiting longer for operations and for services that they used to be able to get quickly.
How can the government expect me to say anything positive about this budget when it has attacked two basic programs essential to the well-being of this country, health and education programs? I cannot and will not say anything positive because I think that the government has not only been dishonest with Canadians, it has betrayed Canadians.
Let me come to another point where the government has had some success through exaggerating the statement about no new taxes. If this were not Parliament, I would be calling it a blatant lie because it is. I have to say that it is a false statement.
I would ask you to ask Canadians whether or not they believe they will be paying more taxes as a result of this budget. Ask them whether or not the goods and services tax that will be implemented supposedly in January 1991 is a new tax that will be implemented during the current budgetary year? Ask them whether or not the withdrawals, the reductions in health, in education and in a number of other areas will necessitate the payment of additional taxes to the provinces, to municipalities, and indeed to individual Canadians. I urge you to ask them.
Of course, we have not even talked about the partial indexation of the income tax. My personal indexation will not keep up to inflation, neither will my salary category on which I pay taxes. There will be more taxes, new taxes paid on those measures because the government has not taken the time to change it to accommodate me and many other Canadians who need this kind of assistance.
Another big distortion is when the government suggested that there will be a growth in the transfer payments according to the growth in population. That is not true. The growth will be in tax transfers. It works this way. I quote from a report I received. "The minister is taking credit for increasing transfers which are really
The Budget
part of the existing provincial tax burden while the federal cash share is down. Total cash transfers for post-secondary education are down $54 million". That is the truth of the matter.
[ Translation]
Mr. Speaker, the Budget reflects the priorities and values of this government. A budget always reflects the priorities of an individual, an organization or a government.
If we look at the increases in certain budgets, we see a 5 per cent increase for Defence and a 20 per cent increase for the Canadian Security Intelligence Service. We see cutbacks in health and education, cutbacks that will affect senior citizens, Canadians who need help and young people who want to work towards a promising future-They say there are no new taxes, which is not true, because the goods and services tax is a new tax. A number of programs enjoy only partial indexation, which is a clear indication that we will pay a lot more taxes- new taxes-on measures that are already in place. Transfer payments to the provinces, to municipalities and to individuals will suffer.
This government claimed there would be no new taxes and that it was entirely fair in allowing certain departments to expand, but it has been extremely unfair in many areas such as health, education, programs for women, aboriginal people, multicultural groups, and so forth.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened intently to my hon. colleague's comments. He joins the masses in opposition to the public outrage against the budget in questioning its legitimacy in a number of areas. The one area I noticed my hon. friend did not mention, because of its very critical importance in terms of the context in which the government places it, is the goods and services tax, a measure which we all clearly oppose.
I just want to clarify one point with my hon. friend. What is the Liberal party's position on the goods and services tax? Is it opposed to the goods and services tax in principle, or just opposed to it for the moment with the hope that maybe later it will have a chance to reap its benefits?

March 5, 1990
The Budget

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to be able to respond to the question. I spoke very quickly when I made my remarks. I assume that is the reason why my hon. colleague did not hear my reference to the goods and services tax. I did indicate how it would penalize students and a number of other sectors.
If the hon. member will recall, in the very recent past I have spoken against the goods and services tax. I have pointed out a number of areas in the health care sector where it will have a very negative effect, such as with respect to psychology services, therapeutic services and so on.
The hon. member is, of course, trying to have some fun with me and my colleagues in this party. He knows clearly that we were among the first and the strongest and the most vociferous against this tax. It is completely unfair for him to suggest that we are perhaps dancing around, that this is perhaps a disagreement in principle. We have said no. I continue to say no, and I shall continue to say no.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not question my hon. friend's sincerity. I think he probably does believe that this tax is a nasty tax.
I have been listening with care to some of the leadership candidates for his party, Mr. Martin and Mr. Chretien to be specific, who both have said: "Well, Mr. Speaker, we are not certain. Quite frankly, something has to be done with the tax system and we will look at it some time in the future." I do not want to suggest to my hon. friend that I am being cute with him, because I believe sincerely that he is opposed to this measure.
What I want him to say is that not only is he opposed, not only has he spoken against the goods and services tax, but in fact the Liberal Party of Canada is in opposition in principle and would never as a government some time in the distant future impose a goods and services tax or a national sales tax on the people of Canada. Is he prepared to say that, to set aside his own personal views and represent the party that he does represent?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot speak for the leadership candidates. The hon. member would not want me to do that.
On the other hand, if I were a leadership candidate I would be saying exactly what I have been telling you. I would not be changing that for one moment. I cannot speak for the party. I can tell you what the party is saying right now.
The hon. member heard, perhaps, this party's critic this morning on Canada AM who will be debating that with the Minister of Finance tonight in Edmonton. He said it was a poor tax. We are against this tax. We have to look at taxation in a progressive kind of way, and we cannot look at it in isolation. I have not heard any of my colleagues, and if you know of any I wish you would tell me, who have said that they are for this tax.
There may be some who are less passionate, less intense about the negative effects. I suspect that is true about any question, but I have heard nothing but complete accord from my colleagues with whom I associate here on this side of the House on that question. We are against this tax.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, where does one begin to debate a budget tabled by the finance minister? The budget contains many measures which will have a devastating impact on students, seniors, native peoples, low and middle income families, war veterans and small business. The list goes on and on.
The finance minister claims there are no tax increases in his budget. He has simply passed on an $8 billion problem to the provinces. Furthermore, the goods and services tax threatens to become the largest tax grab in Canadian history.
The finance minister claims that deficit reduction is not at the expense of social programs. Yet support for medicare, welfare and day care has been slashed. Support for social and co-op housing will be cut by $165 million over a five year period, compounding the problems of the 200,000 homeless in Canada and the many more who must commit over half their income to rent.
Speaking of the deficit, in 1984 the Minister of Finance announced a five year program of deficit reduction designed to cut the deficit in half by the end of the decade. Despite record economic growth, the minister has failed miserably to reach this target. In fact, he has only trimmed $4 billion from the $34 billion deficit that
March 5, 1990

existed in 1985-86, the first full year of Tory administration.
This government is not only bent on destroying the economy of the country, it is also bent on destroying aboriginal organizations which have become, in the government's opinion, too critical of the current administration. Funding cuts to the Secretary of State's budget have been focused primarily on aboriginal organizations. Never has a budget had a more devastating impact on one group. The government has chosen to attack aboriginal organizations because it cannot stand to hear how dismal its record has been in this area.
One has to wonder why one department with a total budget of $3.5 billion has chosen to attack the aboriginal peoples of Canada. The Secretary of State has to cut $23 million from his budget. In reality, when you subtract last December's increase to the department of $13 million the Secretary of State only needs to cut $10 million. Native aboriginal communication societies are hit hardest. Cutbacks to these organizations represent 65 per cent of the Secretary of State's budget cuts. Is this fair? Of course it is not. The government has chosen to eliminate the one program which has served to inform aboriginal Canadians of this government's inadequate handling of aboriginal issues. This government has in effect silenced the aboriginal people.
In my riding, Wawatay Native Communications Society operates a bilingual newspaper, community radio and television stations and a high-frequency trail radio program for trappers. It currently has a staff of 45 people to cover all of the aboriginal communities in northern Ontario, many of which are remote and isolated.
As a result of the elimination of the native communications program and a cut-back in the northern native broadcast access program, Wawatay will lose 33 per cent of its funding from the Secretary of State. Twenty jobs will be lost and Wawatay's award-winning newspaper will most likely become a unilingual English publication. The high-frequency trail radio program will most likely be eliminated.
Native newspapers in this country have contributed to a large degree to the preservation of aboriginal languages. Bilingual newspapers such as Wawatay News have protected aboriginal languages from extinction.
The Budget
Native newspaper publications have also contributed to the preservation of a very unique and distinct culture by publishing a record of aboriginal traditions and customs. Such a record will ensure that these traditions and customs are not lost.
Aboriginal communications societies have made a significant contribution to literacy. Many more aboriginal Canadians are literate today, thanks to native newspapers. This government has bragged about Canada's participation in this year's International Year of Literacy. In my view this government should be ashamed of its contribution.
This Tory government is attempting to destroy aboriginal peoples. This Tory government believes the aboriginal peoples are a thorn in its side. It believes that aboriginal peoples will just go away if funding is cut off.
Canada's aboriginal peoples are living in Third World conditions. Government members often say that I am exaggerating. I have seen these conditions in which some of our aboriginal people live. I challenge members to visit a native community and see the poverty, despair, drug and alcohol abuse, high unemployment, high rates of suicide and violence. Once they have seen these Third World conditions right here in Canada maybe members will understand why it infuriates aboriginal organizations when their funding is cut or eliminated. Funding for aboriginal organizations is crucial to improving these conditions.
The cut-backs in the provinces' transfer payments used for post-secondary education and health care is a direct attack on social programs in this country. Capping increases in Canada Assistance Plan transfers to Ontario, British Columbia and Alberta is an attack on low income Canadians in these provinces. The Minister of Finance has left the provinces with virtually few options -increase taxes or cut services. Students will be forced to pay higher costs toward education. Seniors who are the main recipients of health care in this country will feel the pinch in reduced services. Low-income Canadians will see their already inadequate quality of life eroded even further.
To say the least, one way or another, Canadians will once again be faced with increased taxes as a result of this budget. Whether it be the goods and services tax, the taxation measures from the 1989 budget which came into

March 5, 1990
The Budget
effect this year or provincial and municipal taxes, Canadians will be paying higher taxes.
There are a number of budget measures which directly impact on northern Ontario. The regions of this country are being asked once more to pay for this government's incompetence in managing economic affairs. Small business and junior mining companies will feel the crunch. I can assure this House that that will mean several hundred job losses in my riding. There is no question whatsoever that this government has abandoned its regional development policy.
The cancellation of the Canadian Exploration Incentive Program is a harsh blow to the junior mining industry in this country. Northern Ontario and northern Quebec will lose jobs as a result. While it is still too soon to tell how effective this program was, the government has breached its promise to protect the junior mining industry. Instead, it has contributed to its demise.
The government should have introduced measures which would have made flow-through share investment more attractive. Prior to this government coming to power we had a flow-through share program which encouraged investment in the junior mining industry. Between 1983 and 1988, 35 mines opened in Canada, 16 of which are located in northern Ontario, thanks to flow-through share investment.
When the government introduced changes to the Income Tax Act in 1987 investor confidence declined. To add insult to injury, the government cancelled the mineral exploration depletion allowance. The Canadian Exploration Incentive Program was designed to reignite investor confidence. It was designed to protect the junior mining industry.
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources stated in a press release on February 21 that the federal government is not abolishing the concept of flowthrough shares for exploration. He said that junior exploration companies wall still have the option to obtain equity financing for exploration using flow-through shares. How does the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources expect junior exploration companies to attract investment when the flow-through share program is inadequate?
Analysis of flow-through share financed exploration has indicates that, on average, every million dollars spent on mineral exploration creates some 21 person years of
direct employment. Between 1983 and 1988 this suggests that the $3 billion worth of exploration financed with flow-through shares has generated an estimated 63,000 person years of direct exploration employment in Canada. This alone is proof that the flow-through share program as it existed under the previous Liberal administration was more effective than this government's policies.
Flow-through share funding creates jobs. Given this government's many promises to create jobs, you would think it would be interested in improving this program. Flow-through share funding has led to economic activity in northern Ontario which would have otherwise laid dormant. Flow-through share funding has contributed to regional economic development.
This government has consistently abandoned and destroyed regional economic development since it came to power. It has provided northern Ontario with lip service only. This Tory government will announce some program one year and in the next it either destroys it completely or erodes it to the point where the program is rendered useless.
Regional economic development has become a thing of the past under this government. In his budget speech the finance minister announced that he will eliminate grants to business with limited exceptions. What do these exceptions really mean? Will the government's exceptions be based on financial limits, or based on types of grants?
FEDNOR's future remains uncertain to this day, since we have yet to see the spending estimates for the Department of Industry, Science and Technology. FED-NOR, while not perfect, has served to attract a more diversified economy to northern Ontario. It has served to help small business expand and grow.
I know that my time has expired. I thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I expect the people of northern Ontario to hear more on this budget as time goes on.

speechtext:

When we talk about flow-through shares in Canada and in each province, we could also mention that the crash of October 1987 caused consumers in Canada to lose confidence in the mining industry. I am one of those who defend prospectors in Quebec who are trying to find a new program. Every time we find a new program, we have difficulty implementing it. In my
March 5, 1990

riding now, there is a federal office in Val d'Or that will close. This was ordered by the Minister of Finance.
I would like to ask you the following question: Does Ontario now have programs to help mining exploration as now exist in Quebec? According to the 1867 Constitution, mineral resource development is a provincial matter under section 109.
Do you agree that the province of Ontario should do more to help this sector? Because, as you can see, Mr. Speaker, people no longer trust the federal government to help with mining exploration. Even we on this side of the House have to fight every time, every week, to come up with a new program.
Can you tell me whether the province of Ontario has mechanisms in place to help mining exploration in Ontario?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for the question. The member for Abitibi has a riding very similar to my riding in northern Ontario. These are ridings that have a lot of economic development initiative and which want to get involved in mainstream economics in Canada. Unfortunately there are some difficulties. One is that Ontario governments, Quebec governments and the federal government are not listening to the regions as it relates to mining.
To answer the member's question simply, I do not think that the province of Ontario, the province of Quebec and, in this case, the federal government have put in place the types of programs that will help the mining industry in Canada to flourish and grow.
What I talked about in my remarks to the House and to the people of northern Ontario is this. If we want regions like northern Ontario and northern Quebec to grow we have to put those types of programs in place.
I have asked my colleagues in Ontario to do something similar to what I have asked the federal government to do, that is to put some initiatives in place like the flow-through share mechanism to allow the junior mining companies to get involved in the industry to the extent of creating employment and getting these mines open. I tell the member opposite that there are 10 mines that are ready to go in northern Ontario but no dollars to put in place to get them going. We have the ability but we
do not have the funding. I ask the federal government, as I have asked the Ontario government, to do that for us.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to participate, appreciating that the other member from Ontario made comments about the fact that the Ontario government has not put in place the mechanisms to allow for the economic development of the mining area in that part of Canada. I recognize he complains that the federal government has not done so either. Yet during the whole process leading up to the current legislation on the goods and services tax, many mining industry executives appeared before the finance committee indicating the positive steps that it would have for exploration development of mines, particularly in Ontario but also in western Canada. So I am a little surprised that the member would comment on that.
I would ask the member to tell us just where and how much money he would like to have the federal government kick into this program. It is certainly very consistent and very common in Ontario that the provincial government of Ontario insists on hiring lots of bureaucrats but does not put any money into programs. Here at the federal level we have a deficit problem. We have to deal with some of the problems that are a legacy of the previous Liberal administration.
I would ask the hon. member just how much money he would like from the federal government. Does he have any suggestions as to how much further he would like us to cut back the provincial transfers to make it possible for this to happen?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Conservative government's nonchalant attitude to Canadian youth is deplorable and unhealthy. Although the 15,000 young people in Ottawa-Vanier, my riding, could count on $528,000 in 1987 when the Challenge summer employment program began, they will have to share 4 per cent of that amount, or $23,200,

March 5, 1990
this year. This is even more laughable because it may cost more to administer the program in 1990.
In past years, Mr. Speaker, the jobs created by Challenge and Young Canada Works helped thousands of young people in Ottawa-Vanier pay for their education. Since the devil finds work for idle hands to do, it would be in the Conservative government's interest to invest this money to keep our young people busy and to educate them, which would help it avoid spending millions of dollars on problems of drugs, alcohol, theft and so on caused by inactivity. Mr. Speaker, it is indeed deplorable that the government is cutting its programs for youth.

English]

Mr. Speaker, the announced cuts in the Summer Employment Experience Development Program are going to create tough time for students who want to pursue their education.
The SEED program provides wage subsidies to encourage employers from all sectors to create jobs for high school, college and university students.
Last year in the Ottawa-Carleton area alone, $1.3 million were allocated to the program. This year that amount is being cut by 85 per cent.
Last year 79 jobs were created in Carleton-Gloucester alone. With these cuts, only 91 jobs will be available for students through this program across the whole Ottawa-Carleton region.
In times when fees are going up drastically and the goods and services tax will increase the price of books and resource material, how will students be able to afford an education? The government is denying them employment opportunities and a chance to contribute toward Canada's economic growth.
The government is letting the students down by refusing to invest in our youth and the future of this country.

Mr. Speaker, in May 1989, the Ad Hoc Committee on AIDS was established. It includes members of the House from all three parties and of the Senate.
The Ad Hoc Committee on AIDS is a voluntary group of concerned people who have come together in a non-partisan way to address one of the most serious pandemics facing our world today. This is a voluntary association of committed parliamentarians, but we would obviously welcome the establishment of a special joint committee of both the House and the Senate.
This week we will begin holding a series of public meetings which will result in recommendations to the government. On Wednesday, March 7, Dr. Earl Berger and Mr. Ian Sadinsky, authors of the Working Document for the Development of a National Strategy on HIV Infection and AIDS will appear before our committee. This meeting will be followed by the appearance of the Canadian AIDS Society on March 14.
AIDS represents a serious crisis in Canada. Much has been done to address the many issues surrounding it but much more work still remains to be done.

Mr. Speaker, in 1963 Linda Macdonald, a young mother of five children, sought medical treatment at the Allan Memorial Institute in Montreal from Dr. Ewen Cameron. Instead, without her consent, she was subjected to a series of barbaric medical experiments, including 109 electric shock treatments, being kept in a drug-induced coma, and subjected to a psychic driving tape placed under her pillow.
These projects were funded by the Government of Canada then, as they had been during the 1950s. Linda Macdonald lost the first 26 years of her life. Her lawyer, Tom Berger, has filed an action on her behalf in the
March 5, 1990

Federal Court. I urge the new Minister of Justice to re-examine the decision of her predecessor to deny compensation to Ms. Macdonald and to settle this claim fairly without further legal proceedings.
Despite the white-washed conclusions of the Cooper report and its appalling medical underpinning, Canada has a legal, moral and ethical obligation to Linda Macdonald and indeed to all other victims of these cruel government-funded experiments. Justice must be done.

Mr. Speaker, on February 271 received an urgent message from the Mayor of Umiujaq, Noah Inukpuk, who told me: "The people of the community of Umiujaq, including myself, are suffering terrible hardship as a result of the high cost of living. The pressure on us is incredible. We, the people of Umiujaq, earnestly request that you give voice to our feelings of alarm.
Here are a few examples: a bag of apples that was sold for $2.86 now costs $4.44; bread has gone up from $1.70 to $3.88; a can of evaporated milk, from $1.60 to $2.60; a five-pound bag of flour from $6.13 to $8.36; and pork chops from $10 to $13, and they aren't even fresh".
Mr. Speaker, for several months I have been trying to make the Government of Canada realize that its domestic policy of cutting back on financial assistance is unfair as it affects local air services, as I said in the House on October 23 and 25, 1989.

Mr. Speaker, prior to the recent budget, Canadians indicated they wanted the debt dealt with by cutting government spending, not by tax increases.
The Minister of Finance met the challenge. He responded by cutting and restraining spending in a number of areas, by imposing no new taxes-the first such budget in 22 years. He managed to exempt major transfer
payments to individuals, such as elderly benefits, family allowances, UI and veterans pensions.
Grappling with the legacy of past government overspending is not easy. Those who preceded us never took the unpopular decisions. Their answer was always to borrow some more, to continue to mortgage the future.
I congratulate the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister for taking some difficult decisions, for displaying the determination and leadership necessary to face up to the debt problem and to build the kind of financially stable Canada we want for ourselves and for future generations.

Mr. Speaker, this ad, run in one newspaper today in Canada, cost this government $11,000 for one day. Women's centres are receiving less core funding from this government in an entire year than it is spending on GST advertising. This government's commitment to women is not worth the paper this ad is printed on.
The government is spending $14 million to advertise the GST. Last year the total budget of the Secretary of State's women's programs for one year was $11 million. After this budget, it will be closer to $9 million. The Tories are spending $14 million on propaganda for a tax that no one wants, a tax that has not passed Parliament. They have cut funding to women's centres right across the country that provide support and information to the women of their communities, to battered and sexually assaulted women, to jobless women and to homeless women.
Instead of attempting to silence the voices of women, instead of cutting women's funding by 100 per cent, the GST advertising should be slashed and the Tory government should also be cut by 100 per cent.

Mr. Speaker, the Liberal party continues to stand solidly with Canadians in opposing this government's 7 per cent goods and services tax.

March 5, 1990
To date, with our help more than 600,000 Canadians have petitioned this government to stop the GST. Now, the Liberals are giving Canadians from coast to coast a chance to say no to the GST.
Starting Monday, March 12 through to Friday, March 16 Canadians can vote against the GST by dialling 1-900-720-6052, 24 hours a day. That is right. Starting Monday, March 12 through Friday, March 16 for a mere 50-cent toll charge, Canadians can tell this government no to the GST by dialling 1-900-720-6052.
The Liberals once again take the lead in giving all Canadians an opportunity to tell this government that they reject the biggest, most obscene tax grab in Canadian history, the goods and services tax, by calling 1-900-720-6052. Let us give this government the message, "axe the tax".

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the replacement of the structurally flawed and antiquated federal sales tax is being welcomed with open arms by manufacturers all across Canada. In light of the superficial criticism by others, our Canadian manufacturers see it as the righting of a historic wrong. After all, they have been discriminated against under the existing system for some 65 years.
The implementation of the GST will remove the built-in competitive bias of the existing system, increase capital investment and enhance our ability to compete internationally, according to Mr. Jordan Sullivan, President of Strong Equipment of Woodbridge, Ontario.
Armchair opponents of the goods and services tax should revisit their cursory arguments. Certainly an important initiative such as the GST which will provide an instant 1 per cent to 3 per cent price savings for our manufacturing sector should not be a target for shallow criticism.

Mr. Speaker, this government is taking important steps to control spending,
manage the economy and to invest in the very future of this country. This affects all Canadians.
But let us be realistic. How much control of our affairs will we have if we do not deal with our national mortgage? How much control do we have over our destiny if we owe our souls to foreigners? This government is fighting hard to control spending and regain the very sovereignty lost under the years of fiscal indifference and mismanagement of one Pierre Elliott Trudeau and the Liberal Party of Canada.
If Canada loses its sovereignty and its ability to control its own house, the blame will clearly rest with the seeds and growth of fiscal mismanagement of the Trudeau era.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Tory government is jealous of the popularity of the Liberal Party. It has come up with a new way of recruiting members. Indeed, large numbers of Canadians have taken over riding association executives of Alberta Tory members. They have obviously not done so in order to join the Conservative party, but, indeed, to defeat the government goods and services tax.
By going totally beyond responsible limits of taxation and complexity, and by showing its disregard for the desire of over two-third of the electorate, the government has forced otherwise calm, law-abiding citizens to stand up and say, enough is enough. They have told the government in no uncertain terms, no to the GST.
In addition to phoning the number 1-900-720-6052 in order to oppose the GST, citizens across this country are ready to do almost anything to oppose the GST, including buying membership cards-heaven forbid-in the Conservative party.

Mr. Speaker, this government was elected six years ago with one vital objective, to get control of our nation's expenses. This objective had and has priority over all others because it must. Any other objective cannot be considered, advanced or planned without first having the dollars to do it.
March 5, 1990

The environment needs cleaning up. We all agree with that. But it takes more than political will, it takes money. Our poor and unemployed need the tools and education to make themselves self-sufficient and productive. But that requires more than sympathetic rhetoric, it takes dollars.
Our health care system, one of the best in the world, cannot be sustained without an ever-increasing amount of money. We do not have any money. We are in debt up to our eyeballs. But with this budget, we are finally able to stand on our tiptoes, peer over that mountain of debt and see the future, prosperous and self reliant.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are aware that the 7 per cent goods and services tax will dramatically affect their lives for generations to come, which is why 80 per cent of Canadians oppose the government's decision to impose this cruel and punitive tax on the people of Canada.
Unlike the Liberals, while the New Democrats really do oppose the GST, they also, as a party, offer specific alternatives to the goods and services tax. We did detail explicitly what the government should do rather than impose the 7 per cent tax. This is why I am so disappointed that the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce, sponsoring tonight's GST debate was not prepared to allow the NDP finance critic to participate.
Is it that the Edmonton Chamber of Commerce are not interested in hearing the New Democrat alternatives to the goods and services tax, or is it their fear that the NDP, who have led the fight against the GST across Canada, would point out flaws not only in the government's tax policy, but also reveal that the Liberals really do not oppose the principle of the goods and services tax, as pointed out so explicitly by their leadership candidates, Martin and Chretien.

Mr. Speaker, I returned to Ottawa today having read an article in The Globe and Mail on the weekend about how Alberta is paying too much for Confederation.
I decided to talk about this article with a member of the government on my return to Ottawa. The first cabinet minister's office I saw belonged to the right hon. member for Yellowhead. Not feeling it appropriate to discuss this with an Albertan, I looked around and noticed that not only is the Secretary of State for External Affairs an Albertan, so, too, is the Deputy Prime Minister, Minister of Agriculture and President of the Privy Council, the member for Vegreville.
Now the member for Calgary Centre, an Albertan, is government House leader. Thinking I better tread lightly, I thought I would speak to the government whip, but lo and behold, he is an Albertan, the member for Calgary West.
With the approval of the member for Edmonton- Strathcona, who sits behind me, and the member for Calgary Southeast who normally sits in front of me, I thought I would point this out to you, Mr. Speaker. On the way to the House I wondered what I would do if the Acting Speaker, the member for Edmonton North, was in the chair. With all of these eminently qualified members in this place, no wonder Alberta does not need the assistance provided to those less fortunate provinces.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the minister responsible for the status of women. There appears to be a great deal of confusion between the Secretary of State and the Minister of Finance on the exact impact of the cuts in the recent budget on the existence of some 80 women's centres across Canada.
The minister has stated that she was not sure whether her cabinet colleagues, "were aware of just what kind of services were provided by these centres". The minister knows that these cuts will have a devastating impact on women seeking shelter from family violence, on women seeking education to overcome unemployment, and on women seeking help to overcome illiteracy. Will the minister confirm today that she has persuaded the Secretary of State and the Minister of Finance to restore full funding for these women's centres, or will she admit that she has already failed to stand up for the women of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the brightest future for the women of this country is to ensure that we have a healthy and growing economy and jobs so that women can work towards self-sufficiency and independence. That is exactly what the Minister of Finance has brought down in his budget, and it is a budget which will ensure the future economic help and opportunities for the women of this country.
Let me say as well that the record of this government in supporting women in their aspirations is second to none. The $40 million program to assist women in dealing with family violence goes a long way in addressing an issue which had not been addressed in previous periods of times. There is, as well, the appointments of women, and the work that is done in terms of employment equity.
Everything that this government is doing, and everything that I will be doing in working with my colleagues,
will be to promote equality for women; to work with my colleagues at the provincial and community levels to ensure that services for women and their issues are addressed in an appropriate manner.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the minister has just admitted that she does not consider the women of Canada to be part of our national treasure.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: She said no such thing.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
In his Budget, the minister decided for the first time to restrict payments made to the provinces under the Canada Assistance Plan, without consulting with the provinces and without giving them prior notice as required by law.
The minister knows that children of poor families will suffer the consequences. He ought to know that 48 per cent of poor children in Canada live in the provinces he has targeted.
My question is just this: How can the minister justify his attempts to reduce the deficit if it means the poorest children of our country will suffer.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Leader of the Opposition is entirely wrong.
The provinces are part of the problem. They have to be part of the solution. I can tell the hon. member that the provinces are not going to suffer. Consider the province of Ontario, for example, which has been spending money at 10.2 per cent per year over the last five years, increasing government bureaucrats by 7,014 people while the federal government has been trimming its deficit and trying to get the debt under control.
The hon. member says that the provinces cannot afford it. That is nonsense. They can. It is only about 1 per cent of their budget. Of course they can help with the deficit fight.
March 5, 1990

In the long run it is going to help them because it is going to get interest rates down, and that is what they are asking for.

speakeroldname: Hon. Herb Gray (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister claims that the provinces are part of the problem. Canadians already realize that the real problem consists of himself and his government.
The government wants to cut all funding for newspapers like the Mic Mac News, the paper that played a major role in exposing the terrible miscarriage of justice in the Donald Marshall case.
How many more cases like Donald Marshall will go unnoticed and unexamined because of this government's cuts to native newspapers and broadcasting? Will the Prime Minister agree today to restore funding for native Canadian media and associations, and stop denying native Canadians an important vehicle for justice and full participation in Canadian society? What is the answer today?

Mr. Speaker, this government's record of support for our aboriginal peoples is second to none in the world.
Hon. members will notice in the budget that there were substantial increases in funding for native social, educational and community development projects, in total amounting to an increase of over 8.1 per cent. In so doing the core funding for native advocacy groups funded by the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development is increased and not reduced in 1990.

Mr. Speaker, ten days ago in Halifax this government announced the opening of a $1.6 million office for visiting cabinet ministers. The office is in a plush office tower in the highest rent district. Does the Prime Minister find it surprising that the cost of this office is exactly the amount of the cuts to the women's program in the Department of the Secretary of State? Will he undertake today to cancel this office and restore funding to women's programs.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Dick (Minister of Supply and Services):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the announcement of regional ministers' offices was made about four years ago. It is to eliminate the proliferation of offices that were held in all the minister's constituencies under the previous administration. We now have regional offices in Vancouver, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Ontario, Montreal and in Halifax. This has greatly reduced the cost that was incurred in other places.

It may have escaped the minister's notice but Halifax is not a minister's constituency. I will lend my office to any visiting minister.
My supplementary question is directed to the minister responsible for the status of women. Eighty women's centres nation-wide need to hear from her. Will she make a commitment that women's programs are more important than superfluous cabinet offices and will she at least attempt to convince her colleagues to restore the women's funding?

speakeroldname: Hon. Mary Collins (Associate Minister of National Defence and Minister responsible for Status of Women):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for the Status of Women; Associate Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe I have already answered that question. When you look at the record of this government in promoting equality and opportunities for women, we see the record of employment equity, assistance to battered women and assistance to immigrant women.
Those are the issues that we need to address. Women's centres have been providing services and in some cases they have been receiving project funding. My colleague has indicated that he still continues to have funding for over 550 projects. We will be working with him to address the needs across the country and with provincial, municipal and local activities to develop new partnerships in terms of addressing issues of concern to women and the services that are there. It is not only the federal government acting alone, all of society must work together to address those issues.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Prime Minister. As he knows, women's centres across the country are being closed. Women's publications have been shut down, women's research organizations have been cut back and there is an attempt on the part of this government to silence the voice of women across Canada, whether it is in White-

March 5, 1990
Oral Questions
horse, Yukon, Hay River, Northwest Territories, from B.C. to the east coast.
On top of this, last week when the Minister for International Trade insulted the women of Canada, this was supported by the minister responsible for the status of women in saying that his comments were marvellous.
I want to ask the Prime Minister, who in the election of 1984 and the election of 1988 assured the women of Canada that he stood for equality, for social programs as a sacred trust, and that he would see equality in this country, will he keep that faith today? Will he keep his promise and reinstate funding to women's programs?

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to respond to my hon. friend because I think one of the points that the New Democratic Party has consistently made is that equality comes through economic equality as well. Since this government was elected 1.6 million new jobs have been created and 61 per cent of them have gone to women.
Hear, hear!

We introduced employment equity legislation in 1986. We increased by 100 per cent the number of women in decision-making positions in commissions and agencies of the federal government. We introduced a family violence initiative of $40 million in June of 1988. We improved job training for women as part of the Canadian Jobs Strategy. We introduced a $25 million program for immigrant women, improved child tax credits for low-income families, a plan for equal pay for work of equal value in the federal Public Service and improved pension benefits for women. That is a partial list of the accomplishments of a government deeply committed to the notion of equality and fairness for women.
Since this government came into power we have 1.5 million children in Canada living in poverty; 60 per cent of female-headed households living in poverty and 1 million children waiting for child care.
The mandate for the minister's department describes the minister's role as one which is "to promote equal opportunities for women in all spheres of Canadian life".
Given that women still only earn 66 per cent of what men earn, given that violence against women is increasing in our society, and given that poverty is more and more a women's problem in our society, it is clear that women are still far from being equal. I ask the minister responsible for the status of women as she sees these cuts being made, how is she going to carry out her mandate?
Oh, oh!

Mr. Speaker, inasmuch as the lead question came to me from the Leader of the NDP, I assume there is no objection to my responding.
The question suggested there was an increase in the incidence of poverty in Canada for women and families. In point of fact, the exact opposite has happened since this government has come to office.
There has been a decrease of 757,000 Canadians living in poverty since this government came to office. Included in that number are 229,000 women and 259,000 children. In one year, from 1987 to 1988, the total number decreased by 80,000 people.
On the job creation side, 61 per cent of new jobs have gone to women. With regard to reduction of poverty, 757,000 people have been taken off the poverty line and have been made productive members of society. With regard to the participation of women, starting with the Supreme Court of Canada where there was one woman when we formed the government now there are three. Two women were ambassadors when we formed a government, now there are 13. There were three women deputy ministers, now there are 21.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the minister responsible for the status of women.
In every area of national life the situation of women has been vastly improved since this government came to office.
March 5, 1990

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the Prime Minister.
On December 6, all of Canada was in mourning. Fourteen young women had been massacred in Montreal. However, since that very tragic day, the government has closed women's shelters, cut funds for research and cancelled publications.
Now a minister makes remarks insulting Canadian women and another minister applauds him!
Will the Prime Minister finally prove to women that he understands them, that he listens to them and demand that those two ministers resign?

Mr. Speaker, I attended the funeral following that absolutely horrible and tragic event. I personally communicated with all the families concerned. Since then, I have been in touch with some of the parents affected by this enormous tragedy.
I take it for granted that the Leader of the New Democratic Party makes no connection whatsoever between this great tragedy and the administrative action taken by any government. If she did, that would be cause for concern on the part of all members of this House.
The fact is that the government which I have the honour to lead has more than doubled the number of women in decision-making positions in the federal Public Service. We appointed two more women to the Supreme Court of Canada, for the first time in history. When we took power, there were, I think, two women ambassadors; now there are 13. There were three women deputy ministers; now there are 21.
All our actions, Mr. Speaker, have been directed to the goal of more social justice for women in Canada.
Before I was sworn in as Prime Minister of Canada, there were only two women in the federal Cabinet. We now have six. Since last week, the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada is a woman, for the first time in our history.
The record shows that we care about women, and we will do more to improve the status of women in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. In June, 1989, the Prime Minister said, and I quote excerpts from his address: "We are going to focus more and more on a competitive society. We will concentrate on long-term investment in people, skills training, education, strategic technologies, research and development."
Can the Prime Minister tell us how his budget reductions in transfer payments, in training and retraining funds, in science and technology expenditures, in research and development activities and in student aid will contribute to productivity in this country, to use his own words: "to the creation of a competitive society"? Can he reconcile those cuts with the creation of a more just and humane society?

Mr. Speaker, every single thing that my hon. friend has just said is wrong. In point of fact in all of those areas there have been increases. In all of those areas there have not been cuts. There have been reductions in some areas of the rate of growth.
For the last five years, transfer payments by the Government of Canada to the provinces have exceeded 6.5 per cent while we were maintaining our rate of growth in program spending at 3.5 per cent. While we were trying to reduce the national deficit and cutting 12,000 public servants from the payroll in Ottawa, the Government of Ontario was putting 7,000 more on its payroll and increasing its spending at a rate of 10.1 per cent a year.
That is why we have an inflationary problem in Canada and the member should be addressing his question to the Premier of Ontario and not to the Prime Minister of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, it is rather interesting. If we look at the transfer we find that there is a transfer of funds and tax points. In fact there are fewer dollars.
No!

There are.

March 5, 1990
Oral Questions

Is the Prime Minister willing to meet Education Ministers and other groups such as the Association of Universities and Colleges of Canada, the Canadian Association of University Teachers, the Canadian Teachers' Federation and the Canadian School Trustees' Association, to see what negative impact these cutbacks in funding for education will have in Canada? Will the Prime Minister make a commitment today to meet these groups?

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member had his facts wrong in English and he has them wrong in French. The problem was the same and the solution is the same, in both languages. We are in the process of providing for a new era of increasing prosperity for Canada. We can do more for universities, research centres and institutions across Canada. We have increased our contributions to the provinces by 6.5 per cent annually, while keeping our own increases at 3.5 per cent. I think the provinces must do their share to help the national government and deal with what is basically a national problem. It is not a federal deficit, it is a national one, and all Canadians and all governments have a role to play in this respect.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister. Does the Prime Minister believe his Minister of Finance upheld this noble sentiment when he eliminated the funding five days later for aboriginal newspapers, severely cut back aboriginal radio and television programming, and terminated and slashed aboriginal political organizations?

Mr. Speaker, in regard to the native population, next year the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development will have a budget of over $3.5 billion, which is an increase of $200 million in one year alone. There has been no cut-back to Indians and natives in this country.
There will be an increase of $200 million next year and we propose to do even more in the future.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is also for the Prime Minister. speechtext:

a member of the Conference on Security and Co-operation in Europe in these negotiations?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member and the House will know that during the Open Skies Conference a very important agreement was made involving the four countries which had been the great powers involved in the signature of the Potsdam Agreement and the two governments of Germany. That was important because it filled a void in dealing with some of the implications of German unification.
Obviously there has to be the involvement of other countries including, very actively, Canada. We are one of three nations that maintains a troop presence in Germany and consequently have an unusual interest in some of the implications of unification.
Part of that will be done through NATO. Part of it, as the hon. member suggests, could be done in the context of the CSCE negotiations and discussions which will become increasingly important as we proceed toward developments in Europe. There is also the possibility that informal arrangements can be made involving Canada and perhaps some other countries to become engaged in the process that was begun with the two-plus-four formula.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same minister. We know that the talks on German unification have already begun under the two-plus-four formula but given the fact that Poland has serious and well-founded concerns with respect to its boundaries, has Canada communicated to the six countries within the two-plus-four formula that we will not accept anything short of an absolute safeguard of existing boundaries?

further precision coming particularly from authorities of the Federal Republic of Germany, and Canada is encouraging the Federal Republic of Germany to give those kinds of assurances.

March 5, 1990

Mr. Speaker, I am sure that the friends of the Tory government will be pleased to hear, after watching today's Question Period, that there have been no cuts in this budget.

province has squeezed the poor year after year after year.

March 5, 1990

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Finance my question is for the Prime Minister. On January 29 the Minister of Finance said in this House that about $9 billion in federal sales tax revenue comes from the taxation of business inputs.

speakeroldname: Hon. John McDermid (Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)):

corporate tax burden in the manufacturers sales tax it has been passed on to individual Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I will put my question to the same minister.
As the minister knows, since the signing of the free trade agreement there has been a major haemorrhaging of the border economies through a 19 per cent increase in border crossings and an 85 per cent increase in purchases registered. As the president of the customs union official said, "Canadians enticed by talk of free trade and low prices are heading south in record numbers".
The federal government is proposing to the provinces that if they accept the implementation of the GST, they can now charge provincial sales tax on these purchases. By adding new taxes to the burden already being

March 5, 1990

exercised upon Canadians, is this the way of solving the major haemorrhaging and spending which is taking place and affecting seriously the economies of our border towns and communities?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member knows anything about the free trade agreement, he will know that the increased congestion at the border has absolutely nothing to do with that agreement. As far as the congestion at the border with the trans-border crossings that are taking place and the difficulties being experienced in several border communities, I will be making a detailed announcement to the Canadian Importers Association, the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and others at a luncheon speech this Wednesday in Toronto.

The
minister says it has nothing to do with free trade, but if it waddles, quacks and has feathers it is a duck. In this case it is free trade.
Mr. Speaker, I want to put this question very clearly.
In this year alone we are suffering a $20 billion deficit in our current accounts. That is double what it was last year. Some $3.5 million leaves the economy of this country every hour.
I want to raise this question with the minister: Rather than forcing a new sales tax on Canadians, which will make the haemorrhaging even worse, why does the government not just cancel the tax, cancel the free trade agreement, and give the economy back to Canadians?
Can you waddle and quack at the same time?
