speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the following question will be answered today: No. 175.

Does the government intend to change (a) existing excise taxes (b) existing excise duties (c) the nine per cent sales tax advocated in the Goods and Services 'lax Technical Paper once this tax has replaced existing sales taxes on (i) tobacco (ii) liquor products (iii) transportation fuels and, if not, is the government committed to keeping these taxes at the existing levels in the case of excise taxes and duties and at the proposed nine per cent level in the case of the federal sales tax as advocated by the government and, if so, does it intend to recoup the difference between current revenues from taxes on each of these goods and those projected under the proposed goods and services tax and what will be the new levels of excise taxes, excise duties or federal sales tax for each of these goods?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Holcombe Wilson (Minister of Finance):
speechtext:
Under the proposed Goods and Services Tax, alcohol, tobacco and motive fuels will be taxed at 7 per cent. In addition, excise levies will continue to apply to these products. Given the deficit situation, it would not be
March 5, 1990

realistic to expect that the government would forego the current excise revenues from these items.
The 7 per cent GST rate represents a substantial decrease from the current federal sales tax rates on alcohol, tobacco and motive fuels. The reduction in revenues resulting from this decrease will be only partially offset in the case of alcohol and tobacco products by shifting the imposition of the tax from the manufacturer's to the retail level. Thus, without certain adjustments to excise levies, federal revenues from excisable goods would decline significantly. Sustaining this loss in existing revenues would make the achievement of a 7 per cent GST rate more difficult.
Accordingly, modifications to the rates of some of the excise levies will be made to protect current revenues. Thus, the excise levies on beer, spirits and wine will be increased from $1.58 to $2.29 per case of 24 bottles of beer, from $3.22 to $3.32 per 750 ml bottle of spirits, and from $0.34 to $0.39 per 750 ml bottle of wine. The federal excise tax on cigarettes will rise from $4.28 to $4.36 per carton, with similar increases in the excise levies on other tobacco products. There will be no changes in excise levies on motive fuels.
On average, the prices of these products to consumers should not change as a result of these adjustments.

subsubtopic: MOTION TO ADJOURN UNDER S.O. 52 VIOLENCE AGAINST WOMEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find the request for an emergency debate to be very important and I have written down why I am making this
Routine Proceedings
request. Let me take a few minutes of the House's time to give the reasons.

Today, all women across this land are tuning their television sets to hear from their political leaders that the shock, the pain and too often the horror of words and deeds said against them because of their chromosomes will be brought to a halt because of the political will of our country's leaders in this House of Commons.
Men and women alike, must debate right now in an emergency debate on what we can do to refrain the violence against women. Before we can tackle any debate such as the one on the goods and service tax, the funding for women's groups or the proposed new abortion law, we must be able to demonstrate to the people of Canada that violence against women will not be tolerated.
Men and women must be treated fairly and equally and a message must be sent at once to everyone that there is a strong will in the House of Commons from members to push such measures.
In the years since the introduction of the emergency debate, it is most likely the first time a commoner has asked the permission of this House to entrench fundamental rights for a group of Canadians.
Sexism has reached an endemic state in our country. We are to be blamed because we accept sexism against women as acceptable and understandable and then we accept all forms of violence against women. This abuse must come to a halt, and the proper place to begin right now our journey to fight sexism and violence against the women of our country is right here in the House of Commons.
Today, I am seeking the compassion of the Speaker of the House to allow an emergency debate in order to start a new era of equality among all people, especially men and women of this country.
I therefore ask you, Mr. Speaker, to permit me to move a motion under Standing Order 52(2):
That this House do now adjourn to call on all Canadians to set
aside their differences and pledge that all men and women in
Canada are equal and will be treated fairly.
My motion is seconded by many members on all sides of the House.

March 5, 1990
The Budget

And I eagerly and hopefully await your decision. SPEAKER'S RULING

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no doubt you have had an opportunity after the week's break from the duties of this House to refer to Hansard where I made mention in my remarks about how tough this budget was and how this political party has the political courage and guts to deal with a national debt problem, where others just seem to criticize and do not have much of a resolve as to how we should solve this difficult problem.
It is a difficult time to be in government. This country, plain and simple, cannot afford giveaways. Some segments of the population acknowledge this point; others do not. Hence our job is made that much more difficult.
We are listening and doing what must be done. We have made real progress in restraining spending since
September 1984. This budget is simply a continuation of our fiscal plan.
Over the past five years we have limited the growth of program spending to an average of 3.6 per cent. This is lower than the rate of inflation and lower than any provincial government. That, I deem, is responsible government.
After a generation of double digit growth in program spending by successive Liberal governments, this responsible budgetary approach was long overdue. Between 1970 and 1975 program spending increased by some 18 per cent; in the next five years, by 10 per cent, a period of restraint I guess; and finally between 1980 and 1984 spending on programs was boosted by 14 per cent a year. This budget will once again limit spending growth to well below the rate of inflation. As a matter of fact, except for the interest payment on the debt, this budget reflects a budgetary surplus.
The effect of this budget and earlier restraint measures announced in December is substantial. Spending next year will be cut by $3 billion, and by more than $19 billion over the next five years. This kind of expenditure control is tough but it is needed. Our future, our children's future, and Canada's future depend on our resolve to act today.
We on the prairies know that inflation must be controlled. We understand the effects of high interest rates. We have lived through the disaster caused by the upward spiral of inflation and interest rates some years ago. We are currently feeling tremendous pressure again, and we feel the effects of a stagnant economy caused by a series of droughts and international trade wars. Some money has been cast our way, but this has not solved our problem. Our problem can be solved only with the co-operation of mature, sound federal economic practice and international trade harmony.
We see the effects of rising interest rates today. This budget is a major step toward reducing the federal deficit which will help ease inflationary pressures. Only by reducing inflation can we hope to lower our interest rates. Lower interest rates will also help us further reduce the deficit.
There is no magical or painless solution to the interest rate problem as my colleagues in the NDP would have us believe. We are a relatively small and open economy. We simply cannot ignore the rest of the world and manipu-
March 5, 1990

late our interest rates in isolation. We have to attack the root cause of the problem, and that is of course inflation.
If we fail to control inflation and the deficit we will pay the price. That price is a weaker economy and a weaker government less able to do the things that people want and need. Just as important, we will lose our sovereignty. We could soon see Canada dependent upon the international monetary system. That is something that no true Canadian wants to see, and Canadians have an interest in avoiding it.
The deficit is truly a national problem, a Canadian problem. Therefore it demands a national solution. If we are to restore health to the nation's finances, provincial governments must also do their part. They will also enjoy the rewards of lower inflation, lower interest rates, and sustained economic growth. After all, we do serve the same people.
Substantial deficit reduction cannot be achieved without affecting transfers to the provinces. They are simply too large a part of federal expenses to be ignored. Cash transfers to the provinces alone account for 23 per cent of total federal program spending.
Let us look at the transfer picture. In the fiscal year just ending, tax and cash transfers to provincial governments total more than $35 billion, and these have been growing faster than federal programs generally. They have risen at an average annual rate of 6.5 per cent since 1984-1985. During the same period, spending on federal programs in general has been held to an annual average growth rate of 3.6 per cent, which is well below the rate of inflation.
This year 35 cents out of every federal dollar goes to paying interest on the national debt. The provinces on average pay approximately 12 cents of every revenue dollar toward debt.
In Saskatchewan debt servicing costs are less than 10 cents of every revenue dollar. The Saskatchewan government, under the leadership of Premier Grant Devine, should take great pride in its fiscal record. Given the liability of the farming economy on the provincial treasury and the other factors, it has shown excellent stewardship of the public purse. However, this budget recognizes that transfer payments to provinces cannot continue to expand at the same rates if deficit reduction goals are to be achieved, and they must be achieved.
The Budget
Under the budget's expenditure control plan transfers to provinces are expected to grow by approximately 3 per cent on average over the next two years, roughly the same rate as total program spending.
The budget recognizes the special circumstances of low income provinces too. Transfer income growth in the higher income provinces is expected to average 2.3 per cent, but in Atlantic provinces it will be some 4 per cent over the two years the regime is in place.
The reductions in the rate of growth of transfers to provinces represent about 1 per cent of total provincial revenue. Federal support to provinces remains large and total transfers will still increase to more than $36 billion in 1991.
The poorest provinces will get more growth than others on top of the significant extra help they already get on a per capita basis. As an example, the substantial nature of past transfers has helped Saskatchewan avoid the kind of deficits shouldered by the federal government. This should not change during the two-year period of transfer restraint. The federal government has been careful to tailor the impact of its transfer restraint measures so as to be sensitive to the fiscal capacity of Saskatchewan relative to other provinces.
The Established Programs Financing to Saskatchewan will be limited to the same per person levels as in 1989-1990 for the next two fiscal years, but equalization transfers, which in Saskatchewan are some 60 per cent of the size of the EPF, are expected to continue to grow normally. This means much faster than other federal spending.
Growth of social assistance transfers to Saskatchewan under the Canada Assistance Plan will also be unaffected, because the budget exempts provinces that receive equalization from the 5 per cent cap on growth of these payments.
The result is that transfers to Saskatchewan under these three major programs which total $1.22 billion are expected to rise in the next two fiscal years to $1.25 billion and $1.29 billion respectively. This is less than the increase projected prior to the budget. It does, however, still represent an average growth of about 2.4 per cent over the next two years.

March 5, 1990
The Budget
Federal support to Saskatchewan is going to continue to play a strong, positive role in the provincial fiscal picture. It is worth noting that between 1984 and 1989 provincial government expenditures grew by an average of 4.2 per cent a year, while during that same period federal transfers to Saskatchewan grew by 11.1 per cent annually.
In the next two years the major federal transfer programs will make up close to 30 per cent of total Saskatchewan revenues. In Ontario and Alberta federal transfers account for 20 per cent to 22 per cent of total revenues. On a per capita basis the federal transfers are expected to amount to $1,236 for each Saskatchewan resident in 1990-1991 and $1,269 for the subsequent fiscal year. The same figures for Ontario are $956 and $963.
I am not trying to suggest that these measures will have no impact on Saskatchewan. There certainly will be. However, I believe that the federal and provincial governments must cope with the reality of our present situation. All governments must take actions to ensure that each tax dollar is spent more carefully and used more wisely. All Canadians have to adjust their expectations of what the federal government can deliver, given the present circumstances.
We presently have a national debt of some $350 billion, and it will continue to grow until the year 1995. We can choose to take strong action over the coming years or the matter will be out of our hands.
For residents of Saskatchewan, on balance I believe that the budget can be looked upon as a necessary national effort. It is fair in its demands and promises clear rewards in the form of a healthier economy. Greater financial security for governments and Canadians and a better, more prosperous future for our children are other benefits of this budget.
This budget does much more than reduce transfers to the provinces. It has much to say about continuing restraint within the federal government itself. Canadians want less government and they want less government waste. That is exactly what the government has been doing and is continuing to do with the budget.
The government has placed a great deal of emphasis on restraint and the cost of running the government. Over the past five years this cost has declined by half a billion dollars and is a real saving to the people of
Canada. It represents a reduction in real terms of some 25 per cent.
Government leadership in this area will continue. The 2 per cent cap on non-salary expenditures by all departments has been extended to 1995. This will save the people of Canada $450 million over the next two years. Government departments have taken significant steps forward in their drive to reduce waste and improve efficiency. This process will continue and yield further benefits.
Over all, this budget will reduce spending relative to 1989-1990 levels on about 40 per cent of all government spending on programs, but it is equally important to mention the areas of government spending that will not be affected by the budget. A number of areas have been exempted: elderly benefits, family allowances, veterans pensions and allowances, and unemployment insurance benefits. Of course equalization payments and Canada Assistance Plan transfers to equalization receiving provinces are also exempted. In all these exempt programs will receive an additional $6.2 billion over the next two years, yet despite these major increases in funding to those in need total spending will increase at an average rate of only 3.7 per cent over the next two years. As in the past, our Minister of Finance has sought to spread the burden or restraint over a wide base, yet he has kept in mind-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I can slow down then so that we can all understand what I am going to say, and for reasons of effect, also. I was trying to get as quickly to the conclusion as I could so as not to impinge upon the credibility of your presence here. I will refer back to my notes and hopefully not offend anyone by repeating some very important and meaty matters in my remarks, some very weighty matters.
It is worth taking special note that this budget is about more than reducing transfers to the province. It is about government waste. I made mention of that earlier and I want to emphasize again that this government has done more to prevent waste than any other government
March 5, 1990

before and is courageous enough to want to stick with that.
There have been those who have argued that we are taking the easy way out. I challenge the people who have made that statement because in fact this has not been an easy way out. It has been very difficult. The program to arrive at a deficit reduction formula which will see that Canadians remain happy and at the same time freed from the burden of the national debt is not an easy path at all. As a matter of fact it is very difficult. We say that it will not be terribly popular, but it must be done.
The measures announced in the 1989 budget, together with the spending reductions announced last December and those of one week ago, are absolutely necessary for two reasons. First, they will place the deficit back on a downward path. This will help to free up domestic savings to finance needed investment in Canada. It will diminish our increasing reliance on foreign saving and reduce the burden of debt on future generations.
Second, these measures will contribute in a substantial manner to the lowering of inflation. Only by lowering inflation can we ease the burden on our monetary policy and increase the scope for a downward shift in our interest rates. We simply cannot accept budgetary deficits of $30 billion. The compound interest that we must pay on our debt will suffocate the country. We know that 80 per cent of our debt accumulation since 1984-85 is a result of interest on our cancerous debt. To allow that process to continue would be a grotesque abdication of our responsibility. This budget is a clear indication that we will not stand by and spin this nation into the ground.
I for one-and I am sure there are many-would have liked to have seen us get on a faster path to a balanced budget. However the choices have been made and the path chosen. All members of the House of Commons and all governments must work together to end our nation's legacy debt. It must be the highest priority if we are to pass a strong Canada on to the next generation.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague has made a number of remarks to which I would like to refer. He and others have often identified
The Budget
the supposed high spending of many provincial jurisdictions. In fact Ontario was recently singled out.
My question is as follows: Is it possible that a significant portion of the increased funding by provinces is a result of the cut-backs to provinces in health and education? Those two alone will be over $39 billion between 1986 and 1995. There are also cut-backs to sectors such as agriculture and housing. In fact because of increased poverty which has increased costs to the provinces, is it possible therefore that the increased spending by provincial jurisdictions is a direct result of the reductions in those transfers in a number of sectors?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure to be able to respond to that question somewhat in isolation. I enjoy the conversation that is going on at the far end of the House of Commons. Unfortunately I have to speak while I am on my feet. I would rather choose to listen to see what two experienced colleagues have to say to one another. I do have an answer to at least part of the question. It was somewhat convoluted in that it ties an apparent reduction in federal government spending to an increased requirement by federal governments to come up with extra funding, covering a wide perspective of various budget areas. I will pick two areas in particular that the hon. member made reference to. The two that he made reference to are in the areas of health and education, the perceived reduction in federal government moneys made available to the provinces for those two very important areas.
I want to assure you, Mr. Speaker, that while the federal government has shown that the rate of growth in transfer payments to the provinces is showing a slowdown, the fact is that it continues to grow.
As a matter of fact, had the hon. member been attentive to my earlier remarks, I think he would have found a relationship between the growth of moneys going to the provinces in terms of transfer payments in direct relationship to how we have had to curtail money that we have spent. He would have seen a very dramatic difference between the two, a dramatic difference to the point where moneys going to provincial governments have increased some 6 per cent per annum where the

March 5, 1990
The Budget
amount of increase that we have allowed ourselves is somewhat closer in the order of 3.6 per cent to 3.7 per cent.
First of all, to say that we have restricted funding to the provinces is simply not telling it as it is, with the exception of this year as it relates to their expectations in terms of growth of what they had anticipated.
I have been advised that as of last December, the hon. Minister of Finance, in meeting with provincial finance ministers has indicated to them that this is not a sacred cow in that we, as a federal government, are harnessed with this national debt and are looking for ways to address it. As we have had all kinds of communications from our constituents saying: "Do something about government spending", I think it can be safely assumed that those people who have been writing us mean the same thing for their provincial governments. We have taken the bull by the horns, so to speak, and we have shown a decline in the growth of moneys going to the provinces.
It is interesting to note that we make reference to the province of Ontario. I recall hearing a statistic recently to the effect that only 80 per cent of the transfer payments that went to the province of Ontario, generally understood to be required for the purpose of education and health, went to those two departments. The other 20 per cent went into general revenues.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was with great interest that I listened to my colleague for Regina-Wascana and his statements on the budget. There are a few things, however, that I should mention.
First, his statement that the NDP call for lower interest rates was just an NDP notion. I wish to remind him that the Devine government in Saskatchewan has also called for a lower interest rate policy.
Second, he lauds the leadership of the Devine government in tackling debt in Saskatchewan. I was not able to watch the hon. member's face, but I am certain that there must have been a bit of a smile when he made that statement. Certainly the Devine government in Saskatchewan, as all Saskatchewan people have known, has driven Saskatchewan into its biggest, deepest debt and deficit in the history of our province. It started with a good surplus in 1982, and the last time I tried to estimate it, it came close to around $10,000 per person of debt in Saskatchewan.
I am surprised as well that the hon. member for Regina-Wascana, who has the university in his riding, is not somewhat concerned at the cut-backs which will cost Saskatchewan somewhere between $90 to $100 million in the next two years. It will affect the University of Regina which is in his riding. I am certain the university and students at the university will be making presentations to him to enlighten him of the fact that the cut-backs will hurt higher education in Saskatchewan.
I am also surprised that the hon. member did not mention some of the cut-backs to native organizations. Regina has a major problem dealing with child hunger, particularly among the native community. I am certain the hon. member in his former career as mayor of Regina was very well aware of the problem of hunger in Regina, particularly among the native community. Surely he must realize that this budget will put the extra squeeze on these people.
The last thing I am surprised at, and I would hope the hon. member would make some comment on, is the state of agriculture in Saskatchewan. He knows that the projections are that next year there will be a negative income in the farm community in Saskatchewan. We are facing a serious problem back home. Anybody from Saskatchewan surely has to begin to address that question and the urgent need that farmers in Saskatchewan are facing for some type of support in order to save farm families from going under.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My hon colleague from Regina- Qu'Appelle gives me a great deal to comment on, but I do not believe I have as much time as is required to reply.
I am particularly pleased to note that the member has listened with great interest. It probably goes on record as one of the few times he has ever listened to me with great interest and certainly there has been ample reason why he should have. But I welcome that attentiveness to the House of Commons here today.
I have to make reference to a few of the points that I hastily jotted down. He ridicules the provincial government's ability to handle the finances given to it by public trust. What he does not make mention of is that about the time they were elected, the economy of Saskatchewan was headed into a spiral down hill in that we were to experience low prices for potash, uranium and oil in unprecedented proportions. I do not believe that anyone can point a finger at any political party and accuse
March 5, 1990

politicians of having any impact on the world commodity prices for a provincial commodity.
The fourth item that he alludes to is with respect to the agricultural situation. I have a permit book and no one in this Elouse of Commons has to tell me the drastic plight with which Saskatchewan farmers are currently being confronted. It is a terrible problem but thus far all I have heard is people making reference to the problem, no one has a solution. I would greet with open arms and enthusiasm those who can come forward with a solution to the problem. Perhaps we could build a brick wall around Canada, eat our own wheat. That at least will not cause it to be an international problem.
Yes, the University of Regina does cause me very great concern. As I made reference earlier, 80 per cent of the transfer payments to the province of Ontario went to health and education and 20 per cent went into general revenues. There are no controlling factors on the transfer payments that are going to the province of Saskatchewan which will cost the province $33 million. Let us not frighten anyone with this $100 million figure. It will cost the province of Saskatchewan $33 million and as we have to tighten our belts, I think the province of Saskatchewan can do that.
I would entreat the member for Regina-Qu'Appelle that instead of giving us continued hot air, give us a little rain, it will help out agriculture more than any rhetoric.

The Budget

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: George Orwell is alive and well in Tory ranks.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My colleague from this side of the House just pointed out that George Orwell could not have done a better job than the kind of job that was done on the Canadian people in Question Period today.
This budget is forcing Canadians to take yet another step on the economic tightrope that the Tories have stretched from coast to coast for Canadians. We have had the free trade deal, the clawback on pensions, family allowances, cuts to unemployment insurance, privatization of Air Canada, VIA Rail, now Petro-Canada and Telesat, and the goods and services tax.
All of those things have been heaped on top of all of this. When I say "this", I mean the kinds of things that we were raising in the House today.
This is a so-called budget where the finance minister is attempting to finish the job that he started on Canadians six years ago. I would like to comment to the hon. member for Regina-Wascana that Saskatchewan has been accused of being in violation of the CAP guidelines to provide for those in need, and yet there is no recognition of that in the response that we got from the hon. member for Regina-Wascana.
Saskatchewan has one of the lowest welfare rates in Canada and one of the highest rates of infant mortality. I hope that the hon. member for Regina-Wascana will think about those things the next time he rises in the House and explain how this budget is going to help people in Saskatchewan in view of those horrid statistics.
Because my area of concern is social policy, I would like to talk about the social policy side of this budget.
There has been a cut of $51 million over two years for social housing. This, at a time when Canadians in every major city of this country, in suburban communities and municipalities, and in many cases rural communities are finding it impossible to afford housing in this country. Yet, we have had a $51 million cut for social housing.
The federal government has unilaterally decided to freeze transfers to the provinces for criminal legal aid at the 1989-90 level for the next two years, approximately

March 5, 1990
The Budget
$86 million, at a time when more and more Canadians are unable to defend themselves, to be represented in this great free country because they cannot afford it, because they are living below the poverty line.
The two programs that are most affected by the finance minister's budget are the Established Programs Financing and the Canada Assistance Plan. Under the Established Programs Financing transfer payments to the provinces for health and post-secondary education are made. How much the provinces lose due to cuts to both the EPF and the capping of the CAP program start adding up very rapidly.
British Columbia, my home province, $102 million; Alberta, $98 million; Saskatchewan, $33 million; Manitoba, $38 million; Ontario, $378 million; Quebec, $220 million; New Brunswick, $24 million; Nova Scotia, $29 million; P.E.I., $4 million and Newfoundland, $19 million.
This is at a time when some of those provinces are under tremendous stress. We have heard in this House in the last few months the stress that the Atlantic provinces are under. This is at a time when Saskatchewan is under terrible stress. The hon. member from across the way wanted to throw in the reason that it was drought. If drought it is, then there is stress in that province. Yet, Saskatchewan is being cut by $33 million.
The only reason that there is a balanced budget in British Columbia is that the British Columbia government has not paid adequate welfare rates, has not provided adequate child care, has not provided adequate school lunch programs for those who are poor, has not provided anything in housing, has not provided any of the social safety net features that we expect through transfer payments. That is why that province has a balanced budget.
Now the double whammy is that their cut is even greater and the very people who have carried the province to make it balance its budget are going to be hit again with another whammy.
Under health care, CBC reported that Quebec's Minister of Health may be forced to stop funding some medicare services as a result of the cuts to the EPF. Marc Yvon Cote says that the government's budget is costing
Quebec's health plan $157 million. Mr. Cote wants to drop some services from the universal medicare plan. It would mean more patients would have to pay for some of the treatments and it would mean that that would be right in line with what this Tory government believes should be happening in Canada, that is, the development of a two tier medical system.
British Columbia is already sending heart patients to Seattle for serious, much needed health care. What will the effects of the EPF cuts be to heart patients in other parts of this country? Under the Canada Assistance Plan, transfer payments to B.C., Ontario and Alberta will be capped at 5 per cent more than what they spent in 1989-90. But the anticipated costs are expected to be much higher.
The Canada Assistance Plan came into effect in 1966. It is the federal government's commitment and its responsibility to fund 50-50 the costs of social services and welfare programs in this country. The finance minister is claiming that he is applying the same principle the federal government is using for the clawback of family allowance old age security payments to higher income Canadians. He said that British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario do not need as much help in financing programs as do other provinces.
British Columbia and Ontario, and it is anticipated that Alberta will join in, are taking this government to court, claiming that the finance minister is violating a contract by unilaterally changing the funding formula under the Canada Assistance Plan. The plan requires the government to give one year's notice to the province and requires that the province give its consent.
Under an Order in Council, the B.C. government will be asking the B.C. Court of Appeal whether the terms of the CAP Act of 1970 or a 1967 agreement between the federal government and B.C. give rise to a legitimate expectation that the Government of Canada would introduce no bill into Parliament to limit its obligation without the consent of British Columbia.
It will also ask the court whether the federal government has any statutory prerogative or contractual authority to limit its obligation to contribute 50 per cent of the cost to B.C. of assistance and welfare services.
March 5, 1990

This government is expected to introduce legislation and, indeed, is introducing legislation to change the Canada Assistance Plan Act before the court rules.
Even Leonard Shifrin, a respected columnist when it comes to discussing social policy, has said that this budget is a load of rubbish.
When the finance minister says that the CAP ceiling affects only the three richest provinces, I think it would be important to more accurately say that it affects one half of Canada's poor, who live in Ontario, Alberta and British Columbia. After years of chipping away at universality and claiming benefits should go to only those in need, this government has decapitated the one program that is totally targeted to the poor.
Child care is affected in two ways by this budget. One, the government has failed once again to announce a national child care program. Even more important is the effect of this government's decision to unilaterally change the funding responsibility for a federal-provincial program.
The Ontario Attorney General put it best when he said: "Why would any province in the future ever rely on the undertaking of the federal government to fund a program, if as soon as the program is established the federal government can say: 'Now that you are under way, we have changed our minds'". Since the only way the provinces get assistance for any funding to child care is through CAP, concern has been expressed about whether the three provinces will, indeed, be willing or able to increase funding to address the continuing crisis.
In Ontario, 8,000 eligible families are on a waiting list for subsidized care across the province. The Ontario Coalition for Better Child Care was hoping for 5,000 to 5,300 new spaces for children in the province in the next fiscal year. Now they estimate they may get 1,000, and that would be due to the capping of CAP.
In B.C., as I said during Question Period, it is estimated that 300,000 children need child care and only
20,000	licensed spaces are available. What happens to the other 280,000 kids in British Columbia who need child care?
The Budget
The Native Council of Canada recently reported on the lack of native child care, especially in urban areas, and cited this as a reason for denying natives the opportunity for jobs and education. In Vancouver, it is estimated that there is a native population of 60,000 but there is only one child care centre. It is estimated that
5,000	Indian children are in desperate need of child care, yet there is only one native Indian-run centre called Sundance Day Care Centre.
In response to criticism that his government is neglecting the needs of Canadians and their families, the Minister of National Health and Welfare has always pointed to the child care initiative fund as a shining example of the Tories' commitment to child care. Now they have shown us just how much this commitment means: $1.75 million has been cut from the fund. The department argues that this is only a freeze at the 1989 level of spending, that the $15 million fund was underutilized, the demand was not there. Advocacy groups on the other hand point out that the criteria applied made these funds almost impossible to get. The funding that is granted for more studies does not supply the needed capital or operating funds to create child care spaces for children. This is the only federal program that is specifically for child care and the government has cut it.
I would like to add at this point a comment about the cuts to the veterans' programs. After World War II there was a national consensus that established that those who had gone and fought on behalf of the country, or those who had been willing to go would indeed be given assistance to reassimilate and to survive in society, particularly those suffering from the effects of war.
I cannot believe that this government could be so cynical as to raise the daily charges for vets in long term care from $8 to $14, almost doubling it, and to cut into the very successful Veterans Independence Program. I would like to also point out that the cut to the Veterans Independence Program is another area where women's programs have been cut because many of those veterans have wives at home and the areas that are being cut are going to make it increasingly difficult for those husband and wife teams to remain in their homes.
The average vet in Canada today is in his or her mid-sixties. Their numbers are diminishing. It is incon-

March 5, 1990
The Budget
ceivable to me why this government would cut the programs for the veterans in this country at a time when through attrition those programs are diminishing in cost daily.
In conclusion, it is important for us to note that the cuts in this budget and the way the government has approached this budget are very similar to the way one would try to sucker one's bank manager.
Mr. Speaker, if you or I as small business people went to our bank manager and said: "We have a whole bunch of accounts receivable due us but we are not going to bother about that. We are only going to increase our spending by 5 per cent this year and we are going to try to pay you back and cut down our debt as much as we can, but we are not going to bother those folks who owe us and we are not going to ask those people to pony up what they owe us in accounts receivable.", our bank manager, yours and mine, would think that we had gone off our heads.
This government is introducing a budget. It has all kinds of accounts receivable from 80,000 Canadian profit making corporations that have not paid any taxes, from deferred taxpayers, corporations that have deferred their taxes endlessly and the government increases its budget, cuts in some very important areas where people desperately need the funding, and says to you and I that it is tightening its belt and goes to its bank manager and says: "But we are going to cut our spending where we can".
I would suggest that it is high time this government started asking Canadians on the other side of the economic spectrum to shoulder their fair share of the cuts in this budget and to provide Canada with a balanced budget because I think that it is very important. There is nobody on this side of the House who would disagree with a balanced budget. The difference is the political priority and the priority on the other side of the House is to take the money from the poor, the people who can least afford it, and leave alone the friends of this government. The time has come for this government to share the cost of reducing the deficit in this country and share the cost with its corporate friends, its wealthy friends and not load the burden, yet again, on the poor in this country.

They learned years ago that what this federal government is doing is sloughing off its budgetary problems by reducing the funds to provinces. Years ago, the provinces decided to cut down funding to school boards and hospital societies.
With this type of reduction in transfer payments, what does the member think are the prospects of Surrey Memorial Hospital or similar hospitals getting the necessary funding to solve the 400 bed shortage it has and to adequately staff the beds that they have now?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am privileged to stand in this House and address the question of the budget.
This budget is a blueprint, I suggest, to social and economic disaster. This budget, along with past budgets puts this country on a road that leads nowhere, a road that no one wants to travel except this government.
This budget is not only bad for what it does, but is even worse for what it fails to do. Instead of challenging our people, it penalizes them. This government is turning the future not into a promise but into a nightmare. This government through successive budgets, including this one, is dismantling our country as we once knew it, piece by piece, region by region, sector by sector and person by person.
National programs, national institutions, national services, national partnerships and national commitments are either gone or quickly going. I am afraid that the word "national" may never be found in our dictionary again. If we continue down this road we have to be afraid for our country as we know it.
The latest victim in this budget is the Canada Assistance Plan. As we know, the Canada Assistance Plan is the major vehicle by which the federal government and the provincial governments, along with the municipalities, deliver services to people in this country, services such as post-secondary education, health care, day care and other needed services for our people.
Yet this government again sees fit to essentially forget about the historical significance of this country, to forget about the historical partnerships and agreements that have been set up with other provinces because

March 5, 1990
The Budget
essentially it wants to take its responsibility and shift it to other levels of government.
There are a number of things in this budget that I could speak on, but I want to devote some of my comments to our national commitment on housing or, better put, the lack of, in this budget. The homeless after this budget was presented were not comforted by what was in it. Young working families wishing to buy their first home were not comforted by what was in it. Young single parents looking for affordable housing were not comforted by what was in this budget. They are disillusioned because this government has failed to show some vision and compassion with respect to the housing crisis in this country.
Every weekend when I return to my riding my constituents ask me why the cost of a home in London has risen by over 55 per cent since the Tories took power in 1984. They want to know why millions of Canadians cannot afford their first home. I want to know what the Minister of Finance tells his Etobicoke constituents when they ask him why housing prices in that riding have jumped over 100 per cent in the past five years since his party has been in power.
I want to know how the Minister of Finance explains that increase when the price of a home in his riding rose only 4 per cent in the three years prior to him becoming the Minister of Finance. These astronomical increases in housing prices have occurred all over Canada, from Vancouver to Montreal. But the problem is not limited to large urban centres.
Across Canada the average price of a new home is expected to reach $151,900 in 1990. That means that the average Canadian family would need an annual income of $65,000 or more to reach for the Canadian dream of owning their own home. But in 1988, the average family income was only $46,185. That means that family incomes and salaries must increase by 40 per cent this year before the average Canadian family can own the average Canadian home.
These figures are a clear indication of Canada's growing housing crisis. More and more, Canadians can no longer afford to buy their own home. Rents are rising higher and the cost of shelter is taking up more and more disposable income.
Rather than addressing the problem the federal government is part of the problem. Rather than introducing
measures that encourage the construction of affordable housing this government taxes new housing, especially under its new grief and suffering tax, the goods and services tax. To make matters worse, this government has cut spending on social housing by 15 per cent in this budget in the year 1990.
This is not the first time that the Conservative government has cut funding to housing programs. It is ignoring the 1.3 million families living in inadequate housing in Canada. Instead, the Tories have implemented a policy consisting of cutting programs and hoping that the growing housing crisis will just disappear. It is impossible to make 1.3 million families disappear.
At least 50 per cent of all single parents in Canada are raising their children in unacceptable housing conditions. At least 40 per cent of all seniors in Canada spend their final years in squalor.
There are 1.3 million tenant households that must spend over 30 per cent of their incomes to pay for shelter. Even more astounding is the fact that there are over 600,000 families in Canada that must spend more than 50 per cent of their income on shelter costs.
The Minister of Finance admitted in his budget speech that the cost of housing has increased about 10 per cent each year. In some areas, such as Toronto, the price of a home has doubled in just four years. The cost of rents has matched these increases and jumped at an incredible pace.
With house prices rising in the last 10 years, housing construction has focused mainly on luxury homes and condominiums. Home builders have no incentives to construct affordable housing. In fact, governments at all levels impose barriers toward the building of affordable housing. The supply of affordable housing has decreased dramatically in urban centres during recent years.
Rooming houses are being closed. Affordable units are being converted and older downtown neighbourhoods are being renovated for a more upscale clientele. The poor are forced to move, but where can they go? Private developers build for the most lucrative markets, the middle and high ends. There are no incentives for them to build what is needed most-affordable housing. The government must work with the private sector, not against it, to bring onstream affordable housing. High interest rates, taxes, red tape, lengthy delays and redun-
March 5, 1990

dant regulations are not the answers to our housing problems.
Rental apartments represented just 17 per cent of total dwelling starts across this country in 1988. New private rental construction has virtually disappeared in some centres. While the need for affordable housing has increased at an alarming pace, this government has taken the opportunity to abandon its responsibility.
Here is this government's pathetic record. Just two months after it was elected in 1984, it cut the Residential Rehabilitation Program by $29.4 million and the social housing budget by about $9.6 million. By 1986, RRAP was cut again, this time in half. During this same period total grants and contributions from CMHC would fall by $400 million on an annual basis. The 1989 budget saw the elimination of the rental component of the RRAP program. The government thereby removed essential assistance to landlords to upgrade their properties. Much of the funding for this program went to maintaining our older buildings. Loss of these funds will only hurt the poor, taking away their last source of adequate housing and pushing them into unacceptable living conditions.
In 1986 this government said it was dedicated to supporting social housing. It launched a program to build
5,000	co-operative housing units each and every year. But after three years of failing to meet its commitment, it cut the co-op housing program by 25 per cent, and only 1,900 units were built in 1989. Yet the waiting lists get longer and longer and longer.
What kind of housing program does this government have to offer the 54,000 people in Ontario who are on waiting lists for co-operative or non-profit housing? What government programs are in place for the 14,000 families in Montreal alone who are waiting for public housing? What government programs are in place to help those people in Vancouver, Halifax and even London, Ontario, who are waiting for affordable housing?
Housing costs have increased each and every year at rates higher than inflation, but spending on social housing has been cut by this government time and time again. It has fallen almost 20 per cent in the last five years compared to the 1980-84 period.
The Budget
The Conservative government has been eliminating the housing programs that are most desperately needed at a time when they can do the most good. This government has again cut the desperately needed funds for social housing in this budget. This means that the
54,000	families in Ontario and the 14,000 families in Montreal will still be on waiting lists for public housing.

March 5, 1990

virtually transferring its responsibilities once again from itself to the provinces and in turn to the municipalities.
This country, through its Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation, has been at the forefront of housing. Since 1984 this government has seen fit to essentially not take its responsibility for social housing very seriously.
On the other hand, it should be noted that this government has taken away the dream for those would-be new homeowners to own their first home. How has it done that? It has been done by not understanding that the average person who wants to buy that first home needs to be encouraged by their government. It needs to put in place programs that will allow them to buy that first home so that they in turn can put their blood, sweat and tears into that home and allow the equity to take care of itself.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this budget is a brutal blow to the north and to the aboriginal peoples throughout this land. There is no comfort for northerners in this budget at all.
"No new taxes," says the Minister of Finance. What a sham. What deception. Northerners know how many times this government has increased taxes since it was elected in 1984-32 times. The big one, the goods and services tax, is right on the horizon. This budget is counting on the revenues from the goods and services tax.
Further, by cutting transfer payments to the provinces for health and education the federal government is forcing the provinces into increasing their taxes. If there is a funding shortfall, the provinces will have to make it up. There will likely be new provincial taxes.
Increased provincial taxes affect the northern territories under the terms of the federal formula financing arrangements. Under these arrangements, imposed arbitrarily by the federal government, the two northern territories will have to increase their taxes if the provinces increase their tax rates. They will either have to raise their own taxes or face a reduction in their annual operating grant.
Increased taxes, whether caused indirectly or directly by the federal government, are new taxes. We know who is responsible; it is the federal Minister of Finance.
The minister cannot escape the fact that by ordering the cut-backs he is just as responsible as those who have to implement the cutbacks.
The current federal government has already cut back on the funding it transfers to the two northern territories. Yukon's transfer payments have been reduced by $9 million this fiscal year, by $12 million next year and by $20 million the year after next. The Northwest Territories has been cut back by $110 million over the next five years. The effect in the Northwest Territories in this fiscal year is a reduction of about $25 million.
According to the N.W.T. government, these cutbacks jeopardize the territorial government's ability to stimulate the economy. The Northwest Territories finance minister has called the federal action a disincentive to economic growth. He went on to say:
The timing of the federal announcement couldn't have been worse.
It comes at a time when there are a lot of critical economic and social
March 5, 1990

issues to resolve in the Northwest Territories, each of them requiring
substantial financial investment.
Under the new formula, Ottawa expects the government of the Northwest Territories to increase territorial taxes until they reach and remain consistent with provincial levels. If the territorial government does not increase its own tax effort at the same rate as the provinces, its projected annual operating grant from Ottawa will be reduced.
I want to repeat that these funding arrangements were not reached by agreement. They were imposed by the federal government on the territorial governments.
Also impacting on the north in this budget is the elimination of the Canadian Exploration Incentives Program, which will affect mining exploration. While not as helpful as the flow-through shares program, which was cut two years ago by the current government, it is still a loss.
The north is sick and tired of having to pay more for less. Since 1988 this government's miserly feelings toward the north have been creeping out from underneath the camouflage of concern it has tried to maintain. All the rhetoric about being concerned about the north is just that-rhetoric.
If this government truly cared about northern people, would it have cut back on the subsidy to the Canada Post food mail program to remote northern communities? The Minister of Finance boasted in his budget speech that Canada Post turned a profit. He also said he wants Canada Post and other profitable Crown corporations to turn over more of their profits to the government in the form of dividends. He said that this is to contribute to deficit reduction.
Because of the current government's actions my constituents now have to pay $5 for one litre of milk so that the government can pocket more of the profits of Canada Post. This government is taking food out of my constituents' mouths so it can put more money in its pocket.
If this government truly cared about northern development, would it have cut back the transfer payments to the territorial governments? If this government truly cared about northern and aboriginal people, would it
The Budget
have cut $100 million over the next two years from the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs? Would it have eliminated funding for aboriginal newspapers and cut back on other aboriginal communications? Would it have slashed the funding to aboriginal political organizations? Would it have cut back social housing funds, health funding and legal aid?
This government's obsession with the deficit has blinded it to certain fundamental realities. Yes, we must reduce the deficit, but we must not do so at the expense of the poorer elements of society.
What good purpose is served by cutting funding to the aboriginal communications societies? The government is totally eliminating the native communications program, which had funding of $3.4 million last year. It is cutting back on the northern native broadcast access program by 16 per cent, or $2.2 million.
With these actions, it is causing the death of eight aboriginal communications groups and mortally wounding another seven. The National Aboriginal Communications Society estimates these cut-backs will mean a loss of 100 jobs.
What do these cuts mean for northern aboriginal communications? For the Inuvialuit Communications Society the elimination of the native communications program means a loss of $106,000. With those funds the Inuvialuit Communications Society produces a monthly newspaper for Inuvialuit called Tusaayaksat. The cancellation of this funding means the death of this newspaper.
The 16 per cent reduction in the northern native broadcast access program means a loss of $105,600 to the Inuvialuit Communications Society. These program moneys are used to produce an award-winning television program, Tamapta. The production of this program will now have to be curtailed.
These cut-backs will lead to lay-offs. The Inuit Broadcasting Corporation is going to lose about one-quarter of its funding. It will be cut by about $600,000. The Inuit Broadcasting Corporation will lose up to $400,000 from the northern native broadcast access program. Under this program the corporation produced such series as Takuginal, a children's program, and Takuyaksat, the award-winning series from Baker Lake.

March 5, 1990
The Budget
The elimination of the native communication program funding means a loss of about $215,000. These program moneys are used to produce drama, including the popular Super Shamou series.
The corporation will have to cut down on its air hours and close down part of its operation. Staff will have to be laid off in Ottawa and the northern production centres. Throughout the country the story is the same.
The national media do not cover aboriginal issues the way aboriginal people would like them covered, nor as often, nor as in depth as aboriginal people would like. The national media cannot cover these issues from an aboriginal viewpoint. Furthermore, they cannot communicate these issues in the aboriginal languages. Pulling the plug on aboriginal communications is an attack on aboriginal culture.
For the same reason that the CBC was established-to counter the magnetic pull of the American culture-aboriginal media were established as a counter force to the overwhelming dominance of non-aboriginal Canadian culture with its two official languages and multicultural mosaic.
How many Canadians know that there are 53 aboriginal languages in the country? How many Canadians know that these languages are dying? Only three of the 53 aboriginal languages in this country have a good chance of surviving into the next century. These languages were spoken throughout this country for hundreds of years prior to the arrival of the European explorers and settlers. Yet many are in danger of extinction and a major battle has to be waged against their loss. In that battle for cultural and linguistic survival, aboriginal people need the federal government as an ally and a supporter, but the government has turned its back on aboriginal people.
The federal Department of the Secretary of State spends only $1 million a year on an aboriginal language programs. Compare that to the hundreds of millions spent on the two official languages. Even heritage languages, the languages spoken by most recent immigrants, receive more money than the original languages of the first people.
While I am not speaking against the funding of these other languages, I am saying that the government has to
give priority to the survival, preservation and enhancement of aboriginal languages.
In this budget not only is the government not providing this critical support, it is cutting off the means for aboriginal people to communicate in their own languages with their own people. Quite simply, the government is contributing to aboriginal cultural demise.
Aboriginal people in this country want to know why the government persists in widening the gap between the rich and poor in Canada. They want to know why the government is cutting programs that need catching up. They want to know why they have to pay with the loss of their jobs when big corporations in this country do not pay their fair share of taxes. They want to know why they are being asked to pay with their culture and language when the socioeconomic gap between aboriginal and non-aboriginal people in this country is still so great.
Aboriginal people in this country are paying with their lives for the government's lack of attention to the health, education, employment and economic needs that exist.
Aboriginal youth are killing themselves at six times the rate of non-aboriginal Canadians. Aboriginal babies die in greater numbers and their health, when they do survive, is much poorer than non-aboriginal Canadians. Aboriginal people live 10 years less than the non-aboriginal Canadian.
The government sheds crocodile tears for aboriginal people, pretending that it really matters or it really cares, but these phoney tears are not going to rebuild the shattered lives and broken dreams and hopes of the aboriginal people, abandoned again by a government which is hostile to aboriginal aspirations and is as bent on aboriginal subjugation as the earlier colonial administrations.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak in this debate on the Budget, especially after what our colleagues opposite said about incredible cutbacks by the government and what this government has done. And especially after what my hon. colleague just said about cuts at Indian Affairs. I find that rather surprising, because last night, I heard Liberal leadership candidates answer a question about what they would do about Canada's debt if they came to power.
The Budget
They all said they would cut government spending. And today, they say the government should not make any cuts. Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance pointed out that since 1984, our government has been following a consistent and comprehensive plan to ensure that Canadians can benefit from a rising standard of living and a quality of life second to none in the world. This plan had two major thrusts: first, to put the government's financial house in order, something that had not been done for many years; and second, to foster a dynamic, innovative and competitive private sector. The main challenge, of course, was to regain control of the country's finances. The previous administration's legacy consisted of a monstrous national debt. The government's program spending was out of control, and we were faced with an operating deficit unprecedented in this country's history. In fact, fiscal year 1984-85, the year we took over, ended with a total deficit of $38 billion, of which $16 billion represented the shortfall between revenues and program spending. This was in addition to the cumulative deficit built up during the 20 previous years.
To give you a better idea of the size of the problem, the successive deficits incurred in the 10 years previous to this administration show the disastrous progression of our debt. I think it would be useful to look back, to see where it all started and what the result was. At the end of fiscal year 1974-75, the deficit was $25 billion. The next year it was up to $31 billion. By the end of 1976, the deficit was $37 billion; the year after, $48 billion. By the end of 1978-79, we were up to $60 billion. The year after that, we were up to $72 billion. By the end of 1980-81, it was $85 billion. Not bad! The government was rapidly losing control. By the end of 1981-82, $100 billion, but that wasn't enough, and by the end of 1982-83, it was $128 billion. By the end of 1983-84, it was $160 billion, and by the end of 1984-85, the last fiscal year under the previous administration, we had a cumulative deficit of $199 billion, Mr. Speaker.

speechtext:
And I will tell you about your debt, the $200 billion debt you left us in 1984-85. I suppose you knew that when you borrow money, you have to pay interest. Everybody knows that borrowing involves

March 5, 1990
The Budget
paying interest. And before you borrow, you make sure you can meet your payments.
And now going back to the Liberal legacy of $199 billion at the end of the 1984-85. The Government of the day had therefore completely lost control over its spending and, as I said earlier, seemed unaware of the impact interest payments on its huge indebtedness would have on future administrations.
The interests which the Government must pay on this debt-I hope my colleagues opposite are listening-account for the deficit of some $30 billion which it has declared year in year out since 1986. Without this debt, Mr. Speaker, Canada would have no deficit and could even declare a surplus. In other words, we collect enough taxes to pay for absolutely all the services provided by the Government. Our deficits only represent the interests on the debt. Since then, the increase has varied between 2 and 2.5 per cent, a significant change compared with the previous years.
Our friends opposite are blaming us for allowing the national debt to grow to apocalyptic proportions. It is like the pot calling the kettle black. We are forced to pay the interests on the debt which the Trudeau Government accumulated during its last ten years of tenure and that is the reason why we must continue in this direction and keep the situation under control. As future progress will be seriously compromised by inflationary economic pressures, we feel we must continue to limit public spending, something for which we need the support of all Canadians. Interest payments on the national debt are still the main component of our deficit and these budget measures will enable us to cut it down to $28.5 billion next year. By maintaining our program we expect to reduce the deficit to $14 billion over the next three years and to $10 billion in the fifth year. This means that in five years the government will begin to buy back its outstanding bonds and treasury bills and that the country will be well on its way towards a significant reduction in the national debt load.
The lower deficit will contribute to reduce inflation and that in turn will bring interests down. This is something for which the opposition parties have been clamouring for quite some time, but then it is due to the problems they left us with. A reduced deficit will make Canada less reliant on foreign lenders, thereby shoring up our national independence.
Canadians made it quite clear in recent months that they expected lower public outlays rather than higher taxes. Their message got through to the Minister of Finance and this is why his latest budget reflects this new trend.
The two-year expenditure control program will affect all areas of government spending, excepting of course income support programs for seniors, families and veterans as well as unemployment insurance and the equalization program and the Canada Assistance Plan payments to lower-revenue provinces.
The growth of expenditures for some programs will be capped at 5 per cent for the next two years. These programs relate to science and technology as well as to native and Inuit people. Opposition members describe this as a catastrophe, yet expenditures will rise by up to 5 per cent.
This applies as well to the Canada Assistance Plan for the provinces that do not receive equalization payments and of course also to defence and official development assistance.
Some programs will be frozen for two years. These programs concern established program financing per capita, tax transfers on the income of utilities, the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, Telefilm Canada, the Export Development Corporation and Marine Atlantic.
Some programs were reduced like the Department of the Secretary of State, small craft harbours and the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation.
We also eliminated some projects such as OSLO, for the oil sands in northeastern Alberta, a saving of about $650 million, the Polar 8 icebreaker project, for a direct saving of $84 million in 1990-91 and $62 million in 1991-92.
We also eliminated the mining exploration incentive program. This measure should save us $50 million in 1990-91 and $125 million in 1991-92.
March 5, 1990

Some management initiatives will be proposed for the sake of better expenditure control. Stricter conditions will apply to the repayment of financial aid given by the federal government to business; such aid will no longer be in the form of outright grants.
The government will continue with its objective of privatizing companies where its presence is no longer necessary.
In keeping with this objective, we will sell our shares in Telesat Canada, Nordion International Inc. and Thera-tronics International. We will privatize Petro-Canada. This will be done over a period of five years.
A number of Crown corporations and agencies will be wound up, including Canada Harbour Place Corporation, Canadian Patents and Development Ltd. and the Canadian Livestock Feed Board.
Finally, in addition to the initiatives announced last December, which are expected to contribute $2.8 billion in savings over the next five years, a number of further initiatives are contained in this Budget. They are designed to reduce the cost of government and improve management efficiency.
In all, these measures are expected to save $2.8 billion in 1990-91 and $3.3 billion in 1991-92. Taken together with the spending reductions and management improvements announced in December 1989, the fiscal savings total $3 billion in 1990-91, and $3.8 billion in 1991-92. Over the period from 1990-91 to 1994-95, the cumulative fiscal savings will be well over $19 billion.
Mr. Speaker, this Budget meets the expectations of Canadians. It provides for reducing the federal deficit in an intelligent manner and does not contain any new taxes, at the request of Canadians.
Of course, implementing this expenditure control plan will require patience and understanding on the part of all Canadians, and perhaps especially those who are more directly responsible for the situation facing us today and who so far have kept demanding all kind of increases. They should not forget what Canadians experienced during the 80s when they were faced with spiralling inflation. We cannot afford to bring back the despair, loss of confidence and personal problems caused by interest rates of 20 per cent or more that materialized as a result of this inflationary spiral.
The Budget
So many businesses had to close down because they could not afford the exorbitant cost of financing stagnant inventory. So many Canadians lost their jobs as a result. So many Canadians lost many years worth of savings invested in their homes when they could not afford mortgage rates of close to 25 per cent. Many Canadians will never forget that time, and that is why today, Canadians are better able to appreciate why we have to deal with inflation and the deficit and do it now. It means providing a sound basis for a secure and prosperous future.
To achieve this, we must follow a clear plan of responsible fiscal and economic policies to reduce inflation and create a better climate for lower interest rates.
In his Budget, our Minister of Finance continues to do, not what is easy or popular but what is right for the country.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate that Tory members have to defend their Minister of Finance, but by sheepishly saying that he was doing his best they are only trying to discourage anyone from attempting to find out what this Budget is all about.
First, this Budget is a complete sham, and the Minister seems to be abdicating his responsibilities and transferring to the provinces the burden of the debt.
By passing the deficit on to the provinces, the Minister will hit the poor and the less privileged in Canada. He will also be hitting education programs which, as we know, benefit from transfer payments to the provinces from the Canadian Government.
The Minister of Finance, whom the hon. member is supporting, pushed interest rates up. Since 1988 he has been pushing interest rates up to an unbelievable level. As we know, those interest rates further increase the national debt, something I submit he acknowledges when he quite clearly recognizes that he has been doing extensive research on the level on the national debt over these last 10 years, and he agrees with me that since this Government was elected, four or five years ago, they have increase the debt twofold from some $150 billion to the current $300 billion.
I would like to ask the hon. member whether the interest rates he is justifying so well or so badly will not, in his constituency as everywhere else, have devastating effects on small business loans, on housing he certainly supports as any good member, and if finally the interest rates Canadians have to pay now, nearly 15 per cent for

March 5, 1990
The Budget
consumers, and this is no joke, 15 per cent interest now, when the prime rate is at 13.50 to 13.75. Mr. Speaker, I suggest the hon. member will realize one day that he has to stand up and speak for the average citizens he is representing.
Interest rates are much too high, and what does he do? He supports the Minister of Finance. Well, Mr. Speaker, there are lost causes and this may be one.
I would ask the hon. member what he has done recently to try and convince the Minister of Finance to lower interest rates to a level that might be 2 or 3 percentage points above the American rate, but not 5. Canada cannot compete with a country such as the United States when our interest rates are 5 percentage points above theirs.
So here is my very simple question: What did he do personally to help lower interest rates that are now destroying the Canadian economy, that will lead us down the road to disaster, that is the impending recession?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleague for his question. I think that it is very relevant. He mentioned that I built my argument on debt statistics for the last 10 years, and he said so again. I have been a member of this House for a little over a year, Mr. Speaker, and the same point always comes up: We doubled the debt.
Now my colleague did not follow my whole speech. I explained to him why we were now at around $350 billion. Mr. Speaker, I said why and I think it is elementary that when you borrow money, you must not only plan to pay it back but also plan to pay the interest. It is not given away.
My colleague should explain to us how they were able to borrow year after year such large amounts to finance current operations, which shows very poor management, without planning- Because when he says that we doubled the debt, I suppose that he is accusing us, that he is charging us for the interest on their debt. That makes no sense, or rather it can be explained. When the debt has reached such a point and there are no plans to pay it back, it is quite normal to have such a question and to pass the burden of the interest on the debt to the government in power. Yet, Mr. Speaker, in all our efforts, we must maintain a policy of high interest rates for the simple reason that we are faced with enormous expenditures that must be limited to bring down interest
rates which the Bank of Canada is now using to fight inflation.
My hon. colleague should have thought-it maybe too late for them, much too late-but they should have known, having lived through this experience, that by not controlling inflation, by maintaining interest rates at a lower level, and by allowing inflation to rise, they eventually lost total control over a running away inflation.
Mr. Speaker, I would rather support the Minister of Finance interest rate policy rather than have a recurrence of the disaster we faced in 1981-82. My hon. friend should have listened when I mentioned the hardship that situation caused to all Canadians. A great many businesses went under because they could not live with interest rate approaching 25 per cent. A great many Canadian men and women lost their houses because having to renew their mortgages on their house with interest rates as high as 25 per cent, thereby losing their lifetime savings.
