subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for giving me the opportunity to take part in the budget debate. On a national scale Canadians from coast to coast are questioning the financial policies
March 5, 1990

of this government and the economic situation we are facing. The picture does not look too good.
The public debt has doubled in the past six years of Conservative government. It has risen from $170 billion to $351 billion. In spite of massive tax increases and extensive spending cuts the deficit has continued to rise each year, from $28 billion in 1987-88 to $30.5 billion in
1989-	90. The Tories have gone to the taxpayers 32 times for tax increases, either on income through sales tax hikes or through increased fees from government services.
During its six years in power the current government has boosted federal revenues by 70 per cent, from $70 billion in 1984-85 to an estimated $120 billion for the
1990-	91 fiscal year. What use has the government made of all these increased revenues and saved expenditures. It certainly missed the opportunity to make meaningful reductions in the deficit during the last six years when we were experiencing world-wide economic growth.
The Minister of Finance has made his own five-year projection. What does he see in the future? He sees a deficit reduction to $10 billion by 1995. Also his calculations show that the net public debt will by then have increased to $452 billion. That is a $100-billion leap from the current total. According to his figures, four years from now Canadians will be paying $41 billion in annual interest on the national debt, precisely what it will cost us this year. Of course this is based on the assumption that the finance minister's calculations are correct. This may be a highly questionable assumption given his seriously flawed forecasting in the past.
For example, he forecast that short-term interest rates would average 10.1 per cent. In fact they have averaged 12.2 per cent which resulted in the government paying $6 billion more in debt charges than it had forecast. The assumption that the Canadian dollar would be stable and that interest rates would miraculously drop has also not materialized. The finance minister's current projections are tied to 9.5 per cent short-term interest rates. Private economists expect levels of at least 10.8 per cent. That
The Budget
difference would add at least $2 billion to the minister's deficit prediction.
On a more regional basis, northern Ontario, particularly my riding of Cochrane-Superior, has suffered repeated financial and economic shocks in the past year. Northerners have moved from one crisis to another. They have had to deal with many issues. The 15 per cent export surtax on softwood lumber has caused the closure of seven mills in small industry towns resulting in high unemployment. The reduction in air service to northern towns will affect the quality and level of services in the areas of tourism, disabled travellers, and people requiring medical services in the south.
The repercussions of the GST legislation will result in an increase in the cost of all goods because of the transportation service factor. The elimination of VIA Rail to many northern communities will impact negatively on the tourism industry. The elderly and the disabled who used to use trains because they were accessible and affordable will not be able to do so any more.
The hike in postal rates for commercial customers using the northern air stage network will further erode the purchasing power of natives. The tax benefit for northern and isolated areas is on the brink of extinction for 37 communities in my riding if the recommendation of the task force report is implemented.
The Canadian Incentive Exploration Program which was to provide incentives of $160 million for the exploration of minerals, oils and gas was recently eliminated after being introduced in 1988. Its cancellation today will serve a terrible blow to the mining industry.
The recent budget also took a swipe at the federal government's regional program in northern Ontario, FEDNOR, which provides specialized incentives for rural small businesses in logging, manufacturing, motel resorts, tourism, as well as professional services such as architects, computer and data processing services. They will now be moving in the direction of repayable contributions when new or existing businesses apply for assistance.
The north does not enjoy the essential services that urbanites do. The communities lack the medical, educational, recreational, cultural, and commercial services at

March 5, 1990
The Budget
urban doorsteps. Almost all the incentives which encourage people to stay in the north are now being axed.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I would like to direct your attention to the Department of Forestry for which I am the official opposition co-critic.
On February 23, 1990 the Prime Minister proclaimed the Department of Forestry as a full-fledged department and completed the inauguration with the swearing in of the hon. for Prince George-Peace River as minister. I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate the minister on his official appointment.
We now have a Department of Forestry and a Minister of Forestry but ironically a few days before the Prime Minister's announcement the forestry department's budget was slashed by 23 per cent or $47 million. This is incredible.
To add insult to injury, these cuts took place in one of the department's most sensitive areas: federal-provincial forestry agreements. For months we have been urging the government to complete the federal-provincial agreements which are absolutely vital to the viability of the forests in Canada and to the survival of the forestry industry. These agreements are the muscle of the department. Through them the minister can implement federal forestry policy, and he is able to negotiate with provincial officials from a position of strength. If we remove the financial support which came with the agreements, we do not have much left. It is quite evident that nothing has changed. The Minister of Forestry is in the same position as he has been in the last four years.
However Treasury officials have said, according to a report in The Financial Post of February 23, 1990, that this decline in funding is temporary. If and when new agreements are worked out with the provinces, more federal money will be made available through the department. With all these budget cuts one wonders if those funds will ever materialize.
As a member from the province of Ontario I am extremely concerned with the reduction of transfer payments to my province. Health officials are crying for increased funding in order to offer better services. Our educators are faced with having to pass on huge increases in school taxes just to maintain the actual levels of education: $365 million this year and $680 next year. This is shameful. Talk about passing the buck. The
government is passing a big buck indeed. The federal government is passing its financial burden on to the backs of the provinces.
A few days ago I wrote a letter to the Secretary of State in which I said:
I was shocked and disturbed, as were native communities across Canada, to learn that the S3.4M Native Communications Program (NCP) has been eliminated and the Northern Native Broadcast Access Program (NNBAP) has been cut by $2M.
At a time when there is a resurgence of freedom on a global scale, the Government of Canada is slashing two programs which are vital to the linguistic expression of our native communities and which reflect their culture and tradition.
Canadians are rapidly realizing the serious problem of illiteracy in our society. The native communities are no different. Their native language is an integral part of their legacy and without the operational funds from the NCP and the NNBAP, the survival of their language is in jeopardy.
Now, after painting a picture of bad economic times caused by this government, the GST is coming along to choke Canadians, and serve the final blow. This one Canadians will not forget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I listened very closely to what my friend and colleague from Cochrane-Superior has been telling us about a number of cut-backs. If I may, I should like to focus on the so-called cut-backs in the new Department of Forestry. Just a few days ago, royal assent was given to Bill C-29 to establish a federal Department of Forestry. The new department is the result of a promise made by the Prime Minister in 1984 when he identified the need for a full-fledged ministry, and of a government commitment to husband our forests. During fiscal year 1990-91 the department will give more, not less, support to forestry by spending an additional $4.5 million, for a total of $74.3 million. As my colleague pointed out, forests fall under the jurisdiction of the provinces and we simply cannot ignore that fact. The new department is getting organized and the minister does not spare any effort, particularly with respect to federal-provincial negotiations on a number of programs designed to maintain progress made under previous agreements on forest resources development. The 1990-91 main estimates cannot tell us anything about the outcome of these discussions, but they do indicate that several Economic and Regional Development Agreements are about to expire. This should not necessarily be
March 5, 1990

interpreted as leading to lower regular financial or human operational resources. Two agreements have already been ratified, one with Nova Scotia, $45 million on a 55 and 45 per cent federal-provincial basis, the other with New Brunswick, $91 million also on the same federal-provincial sharing ratio. As well, there was a $3.2 million amendment to the agreement with Newfoundland. Negotiations are continuing with all the other provinces and I can assure my colleague and friend that the federal government is prepared to put about about 55 per cent of the funds required to renew these agreements. These funds will be added to the estimates.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like to read the announcement made by the minister. The 90s will present many challenges to the forest sector, and the new department will have a role to play in reconciling the recreational, environmental and social values of our forests. The forest industry ranks first among our various exports and it must continue to supply wood fibers while taking into account the other forest values not directly related to timber. The department is fully aware of Canadian public concern in that regard. I believe that with the members of the forestry committee, who are all interested in the future of this department, we will give strong support to the minister.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in the budget debate this afternoon and I tell you that after a week spent in our ridings, everyone had a week off from Parliament, but I
The Budget
believe that we all worked in our ridings and met our constituents.
So, Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I would like to make a speech on what my constituents told me when we met and I must tell you that they have several concerns. Of course, those directly affected by the Budget are concerned about the cuts and all those who are not affected fear that they will soon be by this Minister of Finance. In general, we have a problem, namely the deficit and the national debt. There, I have decided to deal with it in a non-partisan way and maybe make a few suggestions and recommendations to the Minister of Finance and the government.
Mr. Speaker, if we look at the last decade, economists, business people, labour unions and politicans, like all of us here, had two points in common on the deficit and the national debt. The first is that their forecasts never came true from year to year and the second is that the deficit and the national debt are too high. I think that we have proof from this Conservative government which supposedly should have solved-It told the people that it would solve all the economic problems, but we still have those problems. It has not changed much and we saw in this Budget the cuts that it proposed just to come up with the same deficit forecast as a year ago.
Furthermore, there are as many solutions to these financial problems as there are economists, business people, unions and politicians suggesting them. My first question is therefore this: Is a Government elected to have a surplus or to serve the people who elected it? I thing we must answer this question. We are elected to provide the people with services. We need money to provide such services, but what would be the use of money if there were no people. Therefore, we must achieve a certain balance. To do so, as Canadians, we need both financial and human resources.
Let us now have a look at our country. Canada is a country which extends from the Atlantic to the Pacific and up North to the Arctic Ocean. Distances are enormous. Weatherwise, Canada is a cold country. Yet, it has an abondance of natural resources. Canada not only has a very small population, but its population is spread over huge distances. Although inhabited by various

March 5, 1990
The Budget
ethnic groups, Canada is a predominantly Anglophone and Francophone country.
Compassion and tolerance are the Canadian way of life. In 1990, we have a deficit of approximately $30 billion. Has anybody wondered whether our human deficit is at least equal or perhaps greater than our financial deficit of $30 billion. I think that we should address this issue. Are 26 million Canadians enough to support our standard of living and operate our system as a democratic and modern society?
They keep repeating that our national debt is higher than that of the other industrialized countries. We don't have to go that far, Mr. Speaker. We can look next door, to the south. The United States has a per capita debt that is lower than ours, but its population is eight times as big. Its territory is smaller and its climate more temperate, it costs less to govern that country.
If our debt is too high, is our population a factor? If we had more people, our per capita debt would be lower. I mentioned achieving a balance, Mr. Speaker, and I think that is where a balance is required. We must not only consider fiscal solutions, we must also increase our population in order to achieve continuing economic stability.
Mr. Speaker, I realize I will not have enough time this afternoon to cover all aspects of how to increase our population, but since we are talking about the Budget, taxation and our financial problems, I would like to start by suggesting ways of controlling our annual deficit and reducing the national debt.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada should change its accounting procedures. Our system of accounting is obsolete. Although, as a government, we ask taxpayers who are in business to produce a balance sheet for their company, the Government of Canada, does not produce a balance sheet in its annual report.
We have two types of transactions: revenues and expenditures. There is no accounting for capital investment.
For instance, when the Government of Canada created Petro-Canada, that year the amount spent was shown as expenditures. What did we get at the end of the year? Revenues minus expenditures: a deficit! In the
government's annual report, Petro-Canada cost nothing. Nothing! Now that the government has decided to sell Petro-Canada, I think it is important to set the record straight, and I will get back to the matter of Petro-Canada and Air Canada later on.
Just think, Mr. Speaker, if business people had to draft their financial reports according to this system, the vast majority of our businesses would be in the red. And that is because capital investment occurring in the same year would be put down as expenditures, without accounting for the business's capital and net assets.
The Government of Canada, therefore, must produce every year a balance sheet with assets and liabilities, as Auditor General Kenneth Dye has been suggesting for the past three years. He had even developed and submitted to the Government a model of this balance sheet, but nothing came of it. I suggest it is very important to implement his suggestion.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the accounting system should operate on this basis, in order to separate operating expenditures from capital expenditures. The cost of servicing the debt should be part of capital expenditures in order to plan and finance a long term reduction of the debt. We must develop a financial plan. For the past six years, we have seen the Minister of Finance re-adjust his forecast every year. We cannot solve our financial problems in that way.
Fiscal arrangements should be considered to reduce the debt. Some Canadians would be willing to pay a little more if they felt that their taxes would be used in part to reduce a debt which is increasing every year. That is what our constituents are telling us.
The current operating budget should take into accounts the political objectives of the Government and determine its policies. The Government should establish its objectives and set up a budget for services. But the whole issue of the debt and the servicing of the debt should be considered in a separate budget with specific policies to handle it.
The accounting system should be set up on this basis so that we can distinguish between operating expenditures and capital expenditures All Canadians they might understand better what the national debt means. The issue is really very complex even for experts, and I am
March 5, 1990

afraid we will have great difficulty understanding all the Estimates the Minister of Finance tables every year.
As I said, Mr. Speaker, servicing the debt must come under the capital budget to allow for the long-term planning of the debt reduction and its financing. The policies involving specific steps to tackle those problems must be understood.
Mr. Speaker, any project with long term market value should come under the capital rather than operating and identified budget. And the method of financing such a project must be specified and identified before it is approved.
Mr. Speaker, if it is decided to build another Museum of Civilization, if such is government policy and if it is determined that we need it, fine, let's do it. But we must determine how much this will cost, and how it is going to be financed, rather than always dip into the same purse. And then, when something is sold, the proceeds are put into the same purse, and at the end of the year the Minister of Finance tells us: "I reduced the deficit by $2 billion." In actual fact, he reduced nothing. As in this case, he did not reduce anything, he merely sold of one Crown Corporation.
Mr. Speaker, it is important therefore that we have a management system that is healthier, better controlled, visible and that citizens can understand.
I realize I am taking some time, but I want to make sure that Canadians and hon. members understand what I am saying, because if we really are to reduce the debt and the deficit, we must take the steps needed rather than the GST or other measures proposed by the Department and the Minister of Finance.
Increasing taxes will not solve the problem. In the end, revenues will decrease because Canadians no longer can afford new or higher taxes.
If the Government decides, under that accounting system to incur a deficit, that is their privilege. They are elected by the people and must be accountable to them. Therefore, they are responsible to the people who elected them, then this is very, very easy. What we are seing is that the Minister of Finance after six years in office is still blaming the Liberals, although we have not been in government for six years and the debt was increased by the Tories.
The Budget
Earlier I heard the hon. member suggest: You cannot blame us for the interests we had to pay on the debt you incurred. Does that make any sense? None at all. The problems will not be solved that way. Propose solutions. In six years the Minister of Finance has not suggested anything new.
Mr. Speaker, another example is obvious. He has just suggested selling Petro-Canada but he did not say how or what he intends to do with the proceeds. He sold Air Canada. I would like to know how much he got for it. I think that company was worth something. It was not something to get rid of on a whim. How much money did the Canadian government get to reduce the deficit or even the national debt? Nothing! We had to give!
This government is so irresponsible that it gives away its assets. But, if we sell off our assets, we will be left with only the liabilities, which would create serious difficulties. It is therefore important and urgent to change our accounting practices before this government rips off the whole nation and leaves us in dire straits since we would not have any assets. That is what it did with Air Canada and other companies it has already sold and what it will do with Petro-Canada in accordance with its ripping-off policy.
I hope my colleagues from all sides of the House will understand the urgency and call on this government to accept the Auditor General's report suggesting a change in accounting practices and an annual assessment of the replacement cost of all government capital assets as in any business. They should draw up a balance sheet and from there propose policies to reduce the deficit and especially to finance the debt and reduce it, because that takes a long-term plan, as in any business.
Mr. Speaker, when you buy a house, you take out a mortgage and have a plan to pay it off. At present, the Government of Canada has no plan and I think it is urgent. If the minister is serious about wanting to solve the debt problem, he should develop a plan right away.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have been interested to hear members speak on the budget this afternoon. It is amazing to hear the difference in the speeches. Every opposition member has complained about budget cuts-how this budget cuts all the programs, complaining about budget cuts here and

March 5, 1990
The Budget
budget cuts there. I have to say to myself, as I heard the comedian Yakov Smirnoff say: "What a country!"
I was in my riding last week. The hon. member for Calgary West and I had public meetings. Everyone said: "You gotta cut more. Get the deficit down. You gotta cut". They all tell me that.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Everybody in Calgary says that?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
They all tell me that.
The member for Hamilton West has to come out. I invite him to come to the Calgary Stampede and to talk to Canadians who know what it is like to balance a budget.
I also heard the members talking about interest rates and questioning the finance minister's forecast for interest rates in the current budget. It was noted that last year's forecast was not as accurate as in previous years. I do not think any finance minister in any country in the world could have forecast the unpredictable interest rates of the past year.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: How did they get there?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Well, all businesses and financial institutions forecast interest rates. That is how they predicate their business for the upcoming year.
When I heard criticism of the finance minister's forecast of an 11.1 per cent interest rate over the year, I questioned that as well. I asked the finance minister how he came to that interest rate forecast. I also went to the 20 leading financial institutions in the country. The banks, leading trust companies and brokerage firms also have to do interest rate and economic forecasts across the country. I asked for the average prediction of those 20 leading financial institutions of Canada for the interest rate for the upcoming year. The average prediction was for an interest rate in 1991 of 11 per cent.
If members turn to their budget documents they will see that the finance minister, in fact, has given a very conservative estimate of 11.1 per cent. He is actually giving a higher rate than is forecast by all those leading institutions in this country which make their money in this game."
The government was elected six years ago with one vital objective-to get control of our nation's finances. This objective has had priority over all others because it must. I just listened to my colleague in the finance
committee who understands the problem of the deficit. We do not always agree on how we arrived at that deficit, the $200 billion legacy left to us by the previous government. Any other objective cannot be considered, advanced or planned without first having the dollars to do it.
The environment needs cleaning up. We all agree to that. It cannot be done without money. It takes more than political will.
Our poor and unemployed need the tools and education to make themselves self-sufficient and productive. That requires more than sympathetic rhetoric. It takes dollars.
Our health care system is one of the best in the world. It cannot be sustained forever without an increasing amount of money. We do not have that kind of money any more. We are in debt up to our eyeballs. With this budget, we are finally able to stand on our tiptoes, peer over the mountain of debt that has been created by previous administrations, and see the future as prosperous and self-reliant.
Every homemaker, business person and every Canadian knows that they can only spend what they earn or they will go into debt. Eventually, that debt has to be paid. Everyone who has been in debt knows that to pay it off requires some sacrifices. With consistent and concerted effort the interest and principal can be paid off and the slate wiped clean.
In 1984 when this government came to office, it was clear that our financial situation was such a mess that there could not be any quick cure. The national debt was $200 billion and the previous government in the previous year spent $16 billion more on government programs than it collected. I would like to tell you just what that means. We came into office in 1984. Not only did they have a $200 billion debt that they had been adding to for the past 10 years, they also had expenditures away up here, built in, indexed expenditures and revenue way down here. That is the legacy we were left with in 1984.
First of all, not only did we have to bring that revenue up and hold those expenditures before we could have a balanced budget, after the mess we were left by the Liberals, we had to get to that point before we could start to pay off the national debt.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
At 20 per cent interest.

March 5, 1990

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Exactly. They are racking up these revenues.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Where have you been for six years?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I will tell you where we have been for the past six years. The member asks where have we been. Where we have been is getting Canada out of the hole created. It is not a quick cure. It took until 1987 for Michael Wilson to bring forward a surplus in the operating account of this government. As this budget shows, we have a continued surplus again, $9 billion surplus this year. By 1995-96 we will be able to attack the principal on the national debt.
Within three years we turned that operating deficit around to a surplus. This year the government will collect $9 billion more in revenue than it spends on programs, that is a $25 billion turnaround, a remarkable achievement in such a short period of time.
Having an operating surplus does not yet get us out of the woods. We still have an accumulated debt of $350 billion, the result of 20 years of deficits, the original $200 billion left to us by the spend-crazy former government, plus the compound interest on that debt. Indeed, 80 per cent of the increase in the debt since 1984 is accounted for by interest charges alone. That explains why despite a growing operating surplus, we have a $30 billion deficit this year. It is all interest.
For anyone in debt there are three choices: increase earnings, cut spending or sell assets. The government has used all three of these methods to make the substantial progress we have made to date.
In the 1970s and early 1980s revenues to the federal treasury were declining because of arcane tax rules, exemptions and loopholes, ad hoc tax cuts, the endemic flaws in the manufacturers' sales tax and the direct and indirect impacts of the 1981-82 recession.
In November 1984 we introduced measures that have increased revenues to the same levels, on average, that were earned in the 1970s. These measures have helped bring down the national deficit from $38.3 billion in 1984-85 to $30.5 billion in the 1989-90 budget, nearly $8 billion. Relative to the size of the economy the deficit has declined to 4.7 per cent of the GNP in 1990, a drop of 45 per cent.
The Budget
We have increased revenues, not by gouging taxpayers but by cleaning up the system. We have made it fairer and more reliable. Implementation of the goods and services tax is a crucial part of this process. Our tax reform policies have worked. There is not much more that needs to be done on that front. That is why there are no new taxes in this budget.
This budget concentrates on spending cuts and decreases in government spending. This is neither new nor surprising. Getting spending under control is an integral part of eliminating deficits and giving us the flexibility to attack the debt.
In every budget year we have been in office this government has reduced spending and kept its growth in check. That is why we now have an operating surplus. Seventy per cent of the deficit reduction was achieved by government spending restraint. Only 30 per cent was the result of revenue increases.
The growth of spending on all government programs and services since 1984 has been kept well below the growth of the economy and the rate of inflation. The money used to meet the cost of the government's operations has been cut from $17.4 billion in 1984 to $16.8 billion today, despite a larger workload. The public service has been reduced by 12,000 person years to the same size it was in 1973, despite a 20 per cent increase in Canada's population.
People have said to me: "Well, that's fine. You tell me you have cut the civil service since 1984 and reduced the civil service by 12,000 people, but haven't departments just replaced some of those people by contract positions?" No they have not. When we removed those person years from government departments, we also took the budget that paid for those people. If anybody wants to hire somebody on contract in their department today they have to find the money from some other source within their department funding.
With tight discipline and good management, program spending has dropped from 19.5 per cent of the economy in 1984 to 16 per cent this year. This is its lowest level in almost 20 years and equivalent to a $22 billion reduction in spending. Since 1984, government program spending has increased by only 3.6 per cent per year, significantly less than the 4.3 average rate of inflation. Controlling government spending has not been easy or painless.

March 5, 1990
The Budget
Programs have been eliminated, including the Canadian Home Insulation Program, the Petroleum Incentives Program and the Cape Breton heavy water plants, among others.
Family allowances and transfers to the provinces had their growth restrained and measures to better target the transfer of money to individuals have been implemented. Payments to Crown corporations have been restrained. The government has sold or reduced its holdings in 18 Crown corporations and eight others have been dissolved. Other Crown corporations such as Canada Post were told to shape up. The post office has turned a $400 million annual deficit into a profit and is continuing to improve its service.
Defence and foreign aid budgets were reduced. Direct subsidies to businesses were scaled down. Make no mistake. This government has cut spending. Last December, the President of the Treasury Board announced further steps to eliminate waste, improve efficiency and save $1.4 billion over the next three years. This was done in part by imposing a freeze on federal government construction in Ottawa, travel restrictions for members of Parliament and public servants, and closures of parliamentary restaurants and some government agencies.
This budget continues that work with its two year expenditure control plan designed to save $2.8 billion in 1991 and $3.3 billion in 1991-92. Together with the President of the Treasury Board's cuts announced in December, these actions will save $19 billion by 1994-95.
The expenditure control program exempts transfers to persons. Pensions, family allowance and unemployment insurance payments will not be affected. There are no cuts to veterans pensions. Following the lead of the successful western diversification program, which is headquartered in Edmonton, the budget takes a more business-like approach to business by eliminating grants and making loan repayment measures more rigorous. This places the emphasis on investing in economic development and not giving handouts to the private sector.
Petro-Canada will be sold. The government will wind up a number of Crown corporations and agencies whose
functions can be handled efficiently and effectively by the private sector.
Grants and contributions paid by the Minister of State for Multiculturalism and Citizenship and by National Health and Welfare are being cut. The plan also caps the growth of a number of programs to 5 per cent a year for the next two years. These include the Canada Assistance Plan payments to the fiscally stronger provinces of B.C., Ontario and Alberta and represents about 1 per cent of the total provincial budgets in those provinces.
Federal support to provinces remains large and the total transfers will still increase to more than $36 billion in 1990-91. My province of Alberta is one of the fiscally stronger provinces that will be affected by the cap, but only if the province chooses to increase spending on social assistance by more than 5 per cent this year. If it does so, then it is no doubt better able to bear the extra cost than the federal government. I was pleased to hear from Premier Getty that the province of Alberta will be able to absorb those cuts with no increase in taxes.
Payments to the Alberta government under the Canada Assistance Plan will still go up from $2.3 billion in 1989-90 to $2.4 billion in 1990-91 and to $2.45 billion in 1991-92. On a per capita basis, Ottawa will still transfer back $972 for every Albertan in 1990-91 and $979 the following year. Obviously, there is an effect on Alberta as a result of this budget. We must bear in mind that this year 35 cents of every federal dollar goes to paying interest on the debt. The provinces, on average, pay only 12 cents of the revenues toward debt. Federal and provincial government efforts must be made to ensure each tax dollar is spent more carefully. The effects can be coped with as all Canadians adjust their expectations of what the federal government in the current circumstances can be expected to do.
This is a tough budget, but it had to be. Continued expenditure reductions while maintaining the level of revenue will bring us to a point in 1995 where our operating surplus will cover that year's interest on the debt. Then and only then will we be able to start paying down that massive debt which has impeded our flexibility and stifled our economic growth.
We have implemented measures in the past six years that have put us on the road to recovery but it is a long, long road and there are many pitfalls along the way. The
March 5, 1990

measures to date, the spending restraints and the stabilization of revenue have worked and will continue to work if we do not lose our nerve.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I find myself in a very peculiar situation as I am not sure whether I am in the same House as I was in Question Period. I heard cabinet minister after cabinet minister get up and deny that there were any cuts. They said there were no cuts, that there were only increases in expenditure.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Including the Prime Minister?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
The Prime Minister also said that. I now have the hon. member congratulating himself and his Tory colleagues for the tremendous cuts in expenditure. Who are we to believe? More critical, who are Canadians to believe? The Prime Minister says one thing, you say something else, the Minister of Finance says something else and Canadians are left bewildered. The member passes off the capping of the Canada Assistance Plan. Alberta can absorb the increase in income assistance rates. What happens when the unemployment rate goes up another 2 per cent as predicted by the Minister of Finance and the demand increases for people on income assistance? What happens when the impact of the cuts in UIC take place where thousands and thousands of British Columbians in my home province have been disentitled to unemployment insurance and therefore have to go to income assistance? How is the province going to absorb that?
In the last five to ten years, the province of British Columbia has balanced its budget on the backs of the poor by cutting income assistance, not maintaining it, by actually cutting income assistance payments; by reducing their transfer payments to hospital boards, to post-secondary education facilities and to school districts. This is going to accelerate with this type of a budget.
The member says a wealthy province can absorb it. Maybe Alberta is in a position where there is an out migration of population. B.C. is in a position where there is an inward migration of population plus a settlement of immigrants coming to this country. Our population is going up and yet our revenues from the federal government are being capped.
I want the member to explain the discrepancy between what he says and what the Prime Minister says. Also, could he explain why he feels there will be no impact on
The Budget
services, particularly services that relate to income assistance, child care, post-secondary education and health, which are under tremendous stress in the province of British Columbia. The one thing I do agree with that the member said is the incompetence of the Liberals. It is true. Their fiscal incompetence is only surpassed by the Conservatives fiscal incompetence.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted that the member has taken the time to agree with me that the federal budget has taken a course of restraint. He objects to the cuts. Perhaps he would not be well received in my riding.
I was pleased also to hear the hon. member congratulate the government of British Columbia for another successful budget and for balancing its budgets over the past years. If we had similar restraints shown in provincial budgets across the country as we have in British Columbia or in Alberta, the economy would be in much better shape. I think particularly of the Government of Ontario which continued to raise their level of expenditures by over 10 per cent a year during a boom period, creating inflation and adding to the level of interest rates.
I commend the member for his acknowledgement and credit given the British Columbia government for maintaining a balanced budget, even in difficult times.
I should comment on his point with regard to what has been cut and what has not. People are no longer buying this garble of NDP members and others trying to mix numbers around. What we are saying is that the government has a serious debt problem, one that has been created in this country over a period of 20 years. We are resolving that problem. The record stands for itself. We are attacking the national debt. The only way to do it is to hold down that rate of increase of expenditures to cut the level of increase of expenditures as we have done while maintaining a stable level of revenue to attack the national debt. We have succeeded.
The Minister of Finance has done a remarkable job in holding down that level of expenditure while maintaining a level of revenues that, in the game plan laid out in his budget address, will allow us in the next three or four years not only to pay the interest on the national debt, but to begin to attack the principal on the national debt.

March 5, 1990
The Budget
This is a remarkable achievement and a remarkable budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask my hon. friend, who sits on the Standing Committee on Multiculturalism and Citizenship with a number of us from both sides of the House, some questions related to that department.
I will quote from the budget. I am not making up this figure. The Tory budget has cut $23 million from this year's Secretary of State budget. This means it has cut essential programs for women, aboriginal programs-$90 million we heard today in Question Period-and, of course, the funding for multicultural programs, including advocacy groups and community programs. Last year they cut out the SILT program for language training which was essential for new immigrants to settle into Canada and cut 15 per cent per year for advocacy groups.
In addition to this, I assume the government still has plans to set up three new bureaucracies, a new multicultural department, a race relations foundation and a heritage language institute that would take a lot of money.
I would like to ask him, first, how he thinks cutting $23 million allows enough money for the minister to carry out the mandate of the Canadian Multiculturalism Act? In my view, it is just sheer tokenism. There is no way he can do it, much less set up a new department.
I would also like to ask him about the increasing intolerance, bigotry, and racism that have been documented in this country. Well over 50 per cent of Canadians say it is on the increase. How does he think this is going to be dealt with when the government is cutting back the very community front-line programs and advocacy groups that are there to deal with this? They are the only hope to get some real movement to improve inter-cultural and inter-racial programs and relations in Canada.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for her thoughtful question. She is well aware that she and I perhaps share much of the same opinion on this issue, which is probably unusual because on many issues, particularly finance, we do not.
With regard to her question about the Department of Multiculturalism and Citizenship's policies on racial intolerance, the minister responsible has done a remarkable job in this area with the budget constraints he has had. I know the member would like more money going to advocacy groups across the country to put their particular cases. What the minister has done, and continues to do, is to influence groups already existing in society, police services and any number of government departments, and to bring racial tolerance into the mainstream of Canadian life. He has not relied simply on advocacy groups, although many of them have done an effective job. Across every department of government he has used his influence and the influence of his department to consider this as an over-all government concern, rather than limiting it to his own department. In doing so, within the budget restraints he has, he has done a remarkable job.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with real anger that I rise today to participate in the budget debate for 1990. Both as a New Democrat spokesperson for the status of women and as the member of Parliament for New Westminster-Burnaby in British Columbia, I find that this budget is really deeply offensive.
This is the second year in a row that the Secretary of State's women's program has reeled under severe cuts by the government. This year women's centres and publications have been targeted for total funding cuts of 100 per cent. Every single last penny of core funding for these organizations that provide their communities with valuable information is gone. Women's centres funding has been cut to zero. That is the best example of the Tory commitment to the women of Canada. It is zero.
Women's organizations have been providing for next to nothing the types of information and services which will cost provincial governments millions of dollars to take on. Women's centres are often the first places that battered and sexually assaulted women turn to for help, information and direction. Women's centres show the women in their communities what resources are available to them. They operate largely with dedicated volunteers.
We have not achieved equality for women in our society. Women still make up the majority of the poor in Canada. In the world, women make up the majority of the poor. Women are still not safe in the streets or in their homes. There is so much more yet to be done to achieve true equality for women in our society. Women
March 5, 1990

are challenging the traditional economic structures that have kept them in their place, in our place.
We are challenging the attitudes of the economics of violence. We are being silenced by a government which is, at best, ignorant and, at worst, hostile to our efforts. We are being muzzled.
By attacking women's and native communications' research, the government hopes to keep women and native people uninformed. This is a prime mechanism to silence these growing movements, the opposition to the Conservative attack on the poor, women and disadvantaged. The government is attempting to silence the voices of women and native people.
The Canadian Research Institute for the Advancement of Women received a 20 per cent cut this year. It released an appropriate media statement entitled: "A woman in justice-but no justice for women". It said that the appointment of a woman Justice Minister cannot substitute for financial support for women's equality efforts. The government appoints women who will parrot its policies, despite their principles and, perhaps, despite their better judgment.
The government has spent more money funding strip clubs than women's groups. It has loaned $17 million to 38 strip joints. The total budget of the women's program last year was $11 million. The women's program funds hundreds of women's resources all over the country.
The Canada Assistance Plan which funds social assistance but also funds shelters for battered women was dealt a blow in this budget. The Tories slapped a spending limit on British Columbia, Alberta and Ontario CAP funds. Shelters for battered women today must turn away one of every two women who appear begging for a space. What is the cap on the Canada Assistance Plan going to mean for these women? Where will they go?
The Canada Assistance Plan is also how child care is funded in our country. In my home province of British Columbia, 280,000 children are in desperate need of child care right now. There are 20,000 licensed spaces. The Tories promised us a brand new child care program before the last election. Instead, it is cutting back on child care. These cuts really do make me angry because they go hand in hand with a $114 million budget increase
The Budget
for the Canadian Armed Forces in Europe. When the Berlin wall has crumbled, when the spirit of openness and co-operation exists now among eastern European people, the Canadian government is stepping up its military forces in Europe at the expense of women, at the expense of children, at the expense of native people and the poor of Canada.
The Tory government increased the budget for security intelligence, increased the budget for CSIS, by $33 million while taking $1.6 million from the women's program. This is in addition to last year's cuts to women's programming of $2 million. The government's priorities are truly disgusting.
This budget, according to the government's own projections, will lead to higher unemployment, to the tune of 100,000 jobs lost per year. This budget contributes to lower disposable income for Canadians. The government clearly does not care a bit about how its policies affect real people's lives, it deals with economic policy in the abstract. Women have to find jobs and they discover that these jobs are hard to find. They discover federal employment equity programs with no teeth to them at all. Women have to find child care and discover waiting lists of up to a year and sometimes longer for a subsidized space.
Women will have to start paying the GST on hygienic products, on children's clothing, on boots, on winter coats, on muffins, on hydro bills and on heat. Let the finance minister hand his "no new taxes" line to the women of Canada who will have to start paying the GST on almost every item and service that they buy.
How can employment equity work in a period of cut-backs when people are being fired, not hired? Employment equity is a program for the hiring and promotion of women and minorities. Because of seniority, those left with jobs after massive job losses are mostly white males. Hiring freezes guarantee that women and minorities will not be hired.
The 1990 budget stands alongside the 1989 budget in which the universality of family allowances and old age pensions was destroyed and where the unemployment insurance system was cut back almost beyond recognition.

March 5, 1990
The Budget
The Tory agenda has not created prosperity but misery. The biggest lie ever told was that the Conservatives are good economic managers. We in Canada are now on the brink of a recession. This is where Tory economic policy has led us.
I would like to take a moment and talk about something of which my colleagues on the other side may be unaware. It is the notion of principles. I can see that the members on the other side are squirming and muttering. They may be saying, "Well, we have principles too", and to be fair, I suppose they do. They might, when in doubt, put the burden on working Canadians, put the burden on middle-income Canadians, or a tax loophole for the rich is a vote at the ballot box.
However, there are some ideas which might be a bit more radical for this government. I thought it might consider the principles of fairness and equity. I thought it might consider something honourable like the value of a promise. Evidently I was expecting too much and I will tell you why.
A couple of years ago, the government decided to award some frigate building contracts. As there are excellent and productive shipyards in British Columbia, these shipyards were hopeful that they would receive some of these contracts. These companies and their workers were not asking for a lot. They did not want all of the frigate contracts, they only wanted to be treated fairly by the federal government. Let us look at how the federal government dealt with the people of British Columbia and let us look at the notion of fairness.
Did the B.C. shipyards get half of the contracts? No. Did they get a quarter of the contracts? No. Did they even get one of the contracts, Mr. Speaker ? No, not one contract for British Columbia. For some reason, the logic of which truly escapes me, the Conservatives thought it would be fair to give each and every one of these frigate contracts to eastern shipyards. Mr. Speaker, I am sure that you can appreciate that the people of British Columbia were very upset at this blatant example of favouritism. They were angered by the cavalier manner in which the federal government dismissed them. Canada is a far-flung country and it is hard to believe that Ottawa really cares about the regions of Canada when one can see such reckless decisions being made.
Keep in mind that this is not an administration that governs. This is an administration that reacts. Somehow, surprised at the furore that this snub created in my province, the Tories did what they always do. They scrambled about and they made yet another of their "sacred trust" promises. They said: "No, of course we did not forget about British Columbia. We will give your shipyards the Polar 8 contract". Now, just a short time later, we see those words were just so much hot air. The budget wiped out this promise to B.C. It cancelled the Polar 8 contract.
We see how much the finance minister cares about British Columbia. We see how the Tories govern. They make one promise to get elected and rescind that commitment when the whim suits them.
I would like to remind the government of one thing. It is not a whim to want to be employed. It is not whimsical to fight to keep your shipyard in your province viable. The finance minister may be talking about some abstract numbers in a ledger book, but what I am talking about is reality and real people who want jobs.
His government has failed the people of British Columbia. This government has said to my home province: "Your jobs are expendable". He has said to them: "My government is not a government that operates on fairness or on equity". It is a government which picks and chooses which promises are convenient to keep and which are to be discarded like old Tory election pamphlets.
Where are the voices of the 12 government members of Parliament from British Columbia? What about the four cabinet ministers who come from my province of British Columbia? What influence do they have with this government? It appears the answer is very clear. They have no influence as far as the people of British Columbia are concerned. The Tories have abandoned B.C.
The Tories have long toyed with the lives of all Canadians and this budget is just one more example of the Tory disregard. Under this budget, the finance minister has given the green light to forcing more and more Canadians into unemployment. He has approved plans which will see incomes falling in the next two years. These are not just idle threats thought up by naysayers. These are projections from their own budget documents. If more unemployed poor Canadians is his idea of
March 5, 1990

prosperity, I really think that he should recheck the definition of the word.
The minister also froze the Canada Assistance Plan payments for British Columbia. Of course, this will hit the hardest on those who have the least. The poor in British Columbia are not less poor than the poor in other regions of this country. They hurt just as badly. They line up in the food banks. I have seen them. I have been there. I have seen the food banks in British Columbia simply and solely for women and children. As I said, this will hit hardest on those who have the least. People in any province who battle poverty need help in breaking out of the poverty cycle.
What the minister has done is to take the poor of British Columbia and to say that they are expendable. It is fundamentally and morally wrong to treat Canadians in this way. The lives of Canadian women and men are not numbers to be pushed over from one column of the ledger sheet to another. They are not statistics to fill up some glossy Department of Finance budget document.
Canadian women and men are people struggling to keep their jobs in the face of industries closing down and moving southward because of the Mulroney trade deal. They are individuals struggling with the burden of 32 tax increases since this government came into power and since we have had this finance minister. They are senior citizens who are struggling to make ends meet, who watch the government hack away at their old age security programs. They are single parents living below the poverty line who will now have to pay another 7 per cent on their children's clothing, on their children's boots and coats. They are workers in a shipyard in British Columbia grappling with the question: did the Conservatives kneecap their industry out of sheer ignorance? Or was this a deliberate attempt to kill off this valuable industry in British Columbia?
I have also thought about that question and I cannot really decide what is going through the minds of those on the other side of the House. I do know one thing. I know that we cannot afford to have our jobs taken away. I know that we cannot afford this GST, this regressive form of taxation which will fall on the backs of middle-income Canadians and poor Canadians. Poor and middle-income Canadians will pay the same amount of tax on a pair of shoes that the millionaire on Bay Street will pay. I know that we cannot afford that. We cannot
The Budget
afford the high interest rates that this government has brought us nor the high unemployment rates.
As a matter of fact, Canadians can no longer afford to be governed by the Tories.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in face of the growing national debt, I would like to ask the hon. member for New Westminster-Burnaby, does she believe that any cuts in any government program ought to be undertaken?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are countless tax write-offs that are available to large corporations under this tax reform that the government has talked about for a number of years. They have just introduced legislation that will make it more attractive for rich Canadians to salt money away into an RRSP, where lower-income people do not have this advantage. There are a number of areas, if the government was really serious about cutting back on expenditures. The increases to the military budget are one avenue that the government certainly could have looked at with a fresh eye.
What this government has chosen to do is target the women and the native peoples of Canada. It has chosen to attack any environmental programs that may have had some significance. It has chosen to try to silence the voices of the women of Canada. It has chosen to try to silence the voices of the native people. That is a deliberate strategy, because the women and the native people in this country have been fighting back against this government's arrogance, torture and lack of consideration for women and the disadvantaged in our society. It is a deliberate strategy because it does not want to hear from these yappy women any more who have been telling it that they do not want these Tory programs, they do not want to have the big heavy foot of the Tory government on their necks any longer.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will not go unnoticed that the hon. member decided not to answer the question. What she would like to put before the House is a list of little fox chases that might distract some people. She mentioned that there could be more cuts to national defence. She herself would know that national defence is not an agency simply to be prepared for a hot war. We must also be there to protect our country against international polluters, to protect our ocean resources, to protect against drugs coming into this country, to protect against terrorism. If the NDP had their way and did away with the Department of National

March 5, 1990
The Budget
Defence, the country would be vulnerable to all those international attacks.
The member gave the specific example of shoes, saying that the rich and the poor would pay the same tax. Since today there is a 13.5 per cent tax on the manufacture of leather products, does she not believe that it might be somewhat more purposeful for those in lower income families, who will be better off after the GST is in place, to pay only 7 per cent rather than 13.5 per cent, or has she some mysterious view that 13.5 per cent is smaller that 7 per cent?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is interesting that the member on the other side would raise that question. There is absolutely nothing that indicates that prices will come down when the MST comes off. There is nothing to ensure that prices will drop by 13.5 per cent. I will be very surprised if right across the board prices come down by 13.5 per cent and go up by 7 per cent.
When we talk about the people who will be paying taxes on their shoes, we are talking again about a regressive form of taxation that puts the burden on the middle income earners disproportionately. This is not fair taxation. This is regressive taxation. Canadians recognize it for what it is and they are fed up with it.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to take part in this budget debate.
This debate is about choices. It is about resolve and commitment. It is about having the presence of mind to take a hard look at the harsh realities we face. The choice is there before us to meet our responsibilities head on, or to look the other way. For too long we have seen governments follow a policy of looking the other way. This was not a viable alternative in the past and it is definitely not a viable alternative now. The test is here. It is before us and we have got to face it with resolve and commitment. We have to dig down deep within ourselves and muster up all of our resources to address the formidable and dangerous monster that menaces our every move. That monster is the national debt.
Every day that the debt goes unchallenged is a day that the debt grows stronger and we, as a nation, grow weaker. It is an undeniable fact that the fight with the debt is a zero sum game. For too long it was allowed free rein. It grew into a powerful force with which to be reckoned. We all know that the reasons for the debt's growth was the adherence to unsound financial policies that had charted a course of destruction.

federal government spending has been held at less than 4 per cent. In fact this year's federal spending will rise by only 3 per cent.
It seems to me that this is not an unreasonable limit to suggest. It is definitely not a cut by any means. Some programs have been frozen for the next two years. In the case of the established programs funding this puts the onus on the provinces to employ better management when they are distributing the money that they now receive. They will still receive increments in case of population growth.
Some programs have been reduced. Areas such as Secretary of State, multiculturalism and citizenship have been affected. Critics cry that this government lacks commitment. This government is creating a department of multiculturalism and citizenship. This does not sound like a lack of commitment to me.
Some programs and projects have been eliminated. The Canadian Exploration Incentives Program has been eliminated. The Polar 8 icebreaker has been cancelled, and the support to the Other Six Leases Operation, or OSLO, as been cancelled. In light of the changing circumstances that are taking place in the world the completion of these projects would not produce the results that they were intended to produce. As such, it is simply not prudent to continue at this time. As beautiful and as labour intensive as buggy making might be, it is not prudent in light of technological changes to continue production in competition with motorized vehicles.
Significantly, we are proposing to privatize Petro-Can-ada. For years we have heard calls for privatization. Many of these calls have come from the chairman himself. I say if Mr. Hopper, the man who runs the company, does not know if the company should be privatized, then I would submit that no one knows. But members of the opposition say: "Man, it is terrible. You should not do this". What we have here is a company that will be allowed to borrow money on the open market instead of coming to the government and asking for funds from the taxpayer. What is so wrong with that?
We see before us a prudent budget. The changes are prudent and realistic. There is nothing untoward in this budget unless, I dare say, it does not go far enough. That is what the people at home are telling me, it does not go far enough. Yet I listened to my hon. friend from British
The Budget
Columbia ridiculing the fact that we are cutting some of the expenditures. The people I have listened to in British Columbia are saying: "You did not cut enough".
The members also cry foul and say that this budget goes too far. They say that this is what the majority of average Canadians believe. I would submit to you that the opposition is wrong, Mr. Speaker. The average Canadian is smarter than that. We know from the explanation of the Minister of Finance in his budget speech that to implement cuts instead of restraint would result in a definite negative impact on the Canadian economy. To impose rash cuts would not be prudent, at this time or at any time. That is why it will take us well into the mid-1990s just to address the deficit problem. We will not be able to tackle the debt until after the deficit is out of the way.
We know that it will be a long and drawn out process. In fact, the members also say, "You have had six years, why have you not erased it already?" It cannot be done overnight.
We know that we must work within a realistic framework. Yet what I hear from the critics is that this government is out of touch with reality. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, who is out of touch with reality when they harp at the government to continue to spend more money, when there is not the money coming in?
It is those folks opposite who are out of touch with reality. These are the same critics who talk about the need for more spending without thinking about from where the money will come. They want action but they do not consider the consequences, and they say they represent the majority of Canadians.
In my most recent householder I provided my constituents with the opportunity to tell me what they thought about government spending on the debt problem. I provided them with an abbreviated balance sheet of the public accounts and asked them to consider what was being done and what they thought might be reasonable areas of change. This was a difficult exercise because I had to condense the public accounts into one source. A great deal of information was left out but, nonetheless, a message came through loud and clear.
That message was: Cut back government spending. My constituents were not asking us to spend more, they were asking us to spend less. The perception was that

The Budget
spending in many areas was too high. The prescription was not tax increases but a reduction in spending.
This seems to bring two problems out into the open. The first problem is that perhaps many people do not understand what is involved in government spending. The second problem is that a significant portion of the people that I hear from usually want me to cut the other guy but not them.
The first problem seems to be one of communication and that can be easily rectified. The second problem seems to be one of attitude. Unfortunately, attitude is not so easily changed. Canadians have been conditioned to expect the government to be there for them from the cradle to the grave. They seem to think that the government can somehow access an unlimited amount of money to help them.
What can we do? We have avoided the calls for across-the-board cutbacks of 5,10, 15 or 20 per cent. We have opted for restraint in most cases. In this our sixth budget we have continued in what is proving to be a successful approach to fiscal responsibility. It is a slow, painstaking process but it is sure and it does not cause undue damage to anyone. We are dealing with the government's finances in a reasonable way.
I say to my constituents of Fraser Valley East, to all Canadians and to this House that it would not be prudent to make across-the-board cuts of from 5 to 10 per cent, as attractive as that might have seemed. This is just as true when it comes to spending. It would not be prudent to continue spending in a reckless manner. A balance must be achieved.
That balance is what has been presented to us in this budget. The minister has felt the pressure from both sides. Programs and commitments must be continued. The minister and the government feel the pressure from those who call for cuts. Spending must be restrained. The minister and this government feel the pressure from those who would have more spending, yet the minister and this government persevere.
There is a way to achieve the balance needed to meet commitments and to deal with spending in a reasonable manner. This Minister of Finance and this government are committed to ensuring that we follow the best route for Canada. We have seen that commitment in the past
five budgets and we see it again in this budget. We see a serious response to a serious problem. The government must be disciplined and compassionate at the same time. We are dealing with a national debt here. It is not simply a federal debt. That is why the government has asked the provinces to share in their responsibility. Again we hear the critics cry foul.
It is not unreasonable to ask the provinces to hold the line on the Established Program Funding for two years. I say it is not unreasonable to continue to limit to 5 per cent the growth in the Canada Assistance Plan. It is not unreasonable to cancel certain projects and make management decisions that include privatization. No, this is reasonable beyond a shadow of any doubt. We are committed to certain programs and that commitment stands, but we are also dealing with a serious debt problem that must be dealt with lest our ability to meet our commitments diminishes entirely.
Yet we have amendments made to condemn this government. It is preposterous. There are no tax increases in the budget, yet we are to be condemned for imposing increased tax burdens on Canadians in this budget. This hits of course at the GST which replaces an archaic and a counterproductive federal sales tax system in place today.
We have imposed limits and management has been tightened. We are condemned for abandoning health care, post-secondary education, veterans and regional development. We refuse to interfere with the Bank of Canada's interest rate policy and we are condemned.
We are acting prudently, and we are to be condemned. It is amazing. Instead of giving money away as if it grows on trees, we are providing repayable contributions, a system that has proven to be very successful in the Department of Western Diversification. Members also say we are abandoning our commitments to regional development.
It seems that the only ones abandoning anything are the members opposite. They are abandoning their senses.
I cannot forget that the New Democrats want to condemn us for failing to protect the environment. I tell them to wait until the Minister of the Environment

brings forward his policy paper later this year. Then let us talk about failure.

speechtext: We waited months and months. He was going to bring it forward in April.

speechtext:

They say that we are failing to protect the family farm. The Deputy Prime Minister and the Minister of Agriculture is spearheading a comprehensive policy review of the whole agrifood industry that will put the family farm on stable and fertile soil. That does not sound like failure to me.
This government has reformed the income tax system. We are providing more actual cash-in-hand to low income Canadians than ever before, yet we are accused of abandoning those who need assistance with child care.
We are helping Canadians, not hindering them. These are successes, not failures. The sky is blue, it is not red. Water is wet, it is not dry. The truth is the truth, despite what members opposite would have Canadians believe.
This government has provided leadership on all fronts. We have worked hard to achieve prosperity for all Canadians. We have been constructive when the policies of the opposition have been destructive. We have acted responsibly with commitment and consistency.
This budget builds on our previous successes and sets the stage for future growth. I believe that time will prove yet again that this government has acted as it always has, in the correct and prudent manner that Canadians have come to respect. I would have it no other way.
I for one would be glad to vote in favour of this budget. I would encourage members opposite to vote for this budget if they really care about our country and what the national debt is doing to it.

about the federal Department of Public Works which directed the purchase of a facility for a Customs and Excise training facility even though Customs and Excise said that the facility in question did not suit its purposes.
